Symphony GitHub Apps privacy statement

Save a copy. Press Ctrl+S (⌘S on a Mac) to keep this page as a file, or print it to PDF. This is version 40 of the statement for the Symphony GitHub Apps; the front door repository, OpenSpineConsortium/symphony-start, carries the same text as its PRIVACY.md.

Version 40, 2026-10-20. This text is also at https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/apps-privacy.html. The Symphony browser extension has a statement of its own, at https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/privacy.html.

Who makes the Apps: Gregory Schwing, trading as OpenSpineConsortium (“the developer”). Questions: the contact on https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/.

Symphony is two GitHub Apps. SymphonyBoard (github.com/apps/symphonyboard) brings the Symphony template, or its claim protocol, into a repository by pull request, afterwards reads one branch of that repository once a day for anonymous aggregates and, where the repository holds the claim protocol without the whole template, offers it, by another pull request, the newer versions the template comes to hold of the files Symphony’s board and control panel run on. Symphony Setup (github.com/apps/symphony-setup) applies up to eight settings to a repository in the adoption run, and stays installed, acting only during an adoption run, until you uninstall it. Both work only through GitHub: nothing of yours goes anywhere but to GitHub’s own API, to your own repository and, as aggregates, to the developer, save a Claude token you lend, with your login and account id, into the pool of the developer’s own organization, which that organization then holds (the control panel, below). This statement says what each App can see, what it writes, what the developer receives and keeps, and how to stop any of it.

What each App asks for, and why

The unit of consent is the installation. Whatever repositories you give an App when you install it (“All repositories” or “Only select repositories”), the App can read what its permissions allow on every one of them, and this statement applies to each.

SymphonyBoard asks for eleven repository permissions: Contents (read and write), to read your default branch and push the branch symphony/adopt and, in a repository with no commit yet, to make its first commit, a README, for the Sync run’s reads of your default branch and of the branch symphony/sync and its writes of that branch (the section on the Sync run), and for the control panel’s writes of a file, as you, which the section on the control panel lists; Pull requests (read and write), to open the adoption pull request and, only when you asked for it on the form, merge it, and for the Sync run to read the pull requests from the branch symphony/sync and to open its own or write its description anew; Issues (read and write), to make the board’s labels and, in a new repository, open the issue “Set up this project”; Checks (read and write), to post the protocol check as a check run where the developer runs the App’s server; Workflows (read and write), because the adoption’s pull request and the Sync run’s bring files under .github/workflows, which GitHub lets no token write without it; Codespaces (read and write), which the control panel’s Tokens page used up to version 13 of this statement to make a Codespace and no longer uses, and which stays on the App until the developer takes it off; Actions (read and write), for the control panel’s buttons that start a workflow run by hand, such as the Tokens page’s “Read use now” and “Add Token” and the presses of its box “Your token”, and its reads of the repository’s workflow runs, their jobs and a job’s log (the control panel, below); Administration (read and write), for the control panel’s Share tab and its Notebooks tab’s “Make private”, each as you (the control panel, below): the Share tab reads the invitations waiting for an answer and, when you press the button that says so, invites a person you name by their GitHub username, or one who asked to join, as a collaborator on the repository, gives a collaborator or a waiting invitation a new role, removes a collaborator or withdraws an invitation, and the Notebooks tab makes a notebook’s public or internal repository private when you press “Make private” and confirm; no adoption run, workflow or other page uses it; Secrets (read and write), for the control panel’s Folders tab, which reads whether the repository’s secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH is set and, when you press Track, saves a drive’s refresh token as that secret, and for the Tokens page on a personal account’s repository, which holds its Claude tokens as secrets of its own, each as you (the control panel, below); Variables (read and write), for the Tokens page on a personal account’s repository, which holds a Claude slot’s settings and the list of accounts (SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS) as that repository’s own Actions variables, and for the Folders tab’s Track, which sets the repository’s variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE so that the drive sync’s schedule runs there, as the tab also does when it opens a repository that tracks a drive already, each as you (the control panel, below); and Metadata (read), which every App has, to list the repositories it reaches. It subscribes to five event types (issues, issue comments, pull requests, pushes and check suites), which GitHub delivers only while the App’s webhook is turned on; as this statement is written, it is turned off, and the section on the server below applies from the day it is turned on.

When it adopts the whole template into a new repository, SymphonyBoard makes a second token for that repository alone with Checks read-only. With it, the run reads the check runs named “check” on the commit it pushed to the branch symphony/adopt, only to see whether GitHub Actions has reported that check, for up to ten minutes. It keeps nothing it reads and revokes the token when the settings step ends.

On an organization, SymphonyBoard also asks for two organization permissions: Secrets (read and write) and Variables (read and write), for the control panel’s Tokens page, which saves a Claude account’s token as one of the organization’s Actions secrets, and Secrets and Variables for the Folders tab’s Track in an organization’s repository, which saves a drive’s refresh token as the organization’s secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH and the drive’s id as its variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID, and adds the repository to the repositories that may read them (the control panel, below). A page you are signed in to makes those writes, as you, where you are an owner of the organization. What the App itself writes is in the organization’s pool of Claude tokens, and only there: where someone lends a token through the Token workflow, from the Tokens page where they are not an owner of the organization or from an issue whoever they are (the control panel, below), the organization’s own Token workflow makes the writes for them, on SymphonyBoard’s installation token: one organization secret, the next free slot SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_n, and two organization variables, the list SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, which holds the settings of every slot (for this one, a random id, the login and the account id of the person who lent it and, for a token lent with no say, the word organization). The workflow adds each repository the token is lent to to the lists of repositories that may read the secret and the two variables, and takes a repository off the variables’ lists only when a lender asks to take their own token back from it, whether or not their token reached it, or deletes their token (the control panel, below), and no other of the numbered slots SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32 reaches it, none of them being on in every repository or in every private one, the workflow not counting the slot main, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, whose reach it does not read, so that a repository only that secret still reaches loses the two variables too. So every lender’s login and account id reach every repository a token was ever lent to and every repository an owner’s Tokens page showed while it saved a token’s settings or removed a slot (the control panel, below), save one the workflow took off so or an owner took off by hand, or every repository, or every private one, where an owner set the variables so. The repository’s Claude workflows pass those settings to their steps, and GitHub prints a step’s settings in its run’s log, which anyone can read on a public repository; the one that answers a mention of @claude starts its job only where GitHub marks whoever wrote the comment, the review or the issue that mentions it as the repository’s owner, a member of its organization or a collaborator, so for anyone else’s mention GitHub still lists a run but marks its job skipped: no runner starts, no step runs or prints the settings, and the Claude token is not used. The Token workflow itself, on SymphonyBoard’s token, reads the names and records of the organization’s Actions secrets, never a value, which GitHub gives no one, to find a free slot and which slots hold a token; the public key GitHub gives for sealing them; the records of the two variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, which hold their values, the second with the login of each slot’s owner and, where it holds one, their account id; and the public GitHub record of the person it acts for, for their account id. For a lend with no say it reads the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO, where the owners list the repositories such a token runs on; where the control panel names another of the organization’s repositories to lend the token to (below), it reads that repository’s record and the person’s permission on it; and, for the person’s own token alone, it lists the repositories the token reaches, takes it off one or deletes it, reading for the last two which repositories each other numbered slot of the pool, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32, reaches, never which the slot main reaches, in the run’s memory alone, to know whether to take the two variables off. The Claude token is held on the runner, in a file only the runner’s user can read, from the sign-in to the step that seals it and writes the sealed box to GitHub and then deletes the file; it is never printed, posted or readable from GitHub. The App writes no other secret or variable of its own. GitHub never gives a secret’s value back to anyone, the App included.

The Token workflow can mint SymphonyBoard’s token only where the App’s private key is, which, as the section on keys says, is the developer’s own repositories. So, as this statement is written, the only pool the App writes is the one of the developer’s own organization, OpenSpineConsortium: a token lent there, from the page or from an issue, is held by the developer’s organization as an Actions secret its workflows run on, which its owners, the developer among them, place and delete and which GitHub never shows them, beside the lender’s login and account id, which they see; as with any Actions secret, whoever may write to a repository it is lent to, the developer among them, can have a workflow there use the token or send it elsewhere. The developer’s collector receives nothing of it. Anywhere else, where the repository has no Actions variable SDLC_APP_ID, which names the App beside its key, the Token workflow’s two jobs that would use the key, the one that stores a token into the organization’s pool for its lender and the one that manages a token there, do not run, in the Token workflow as the template holds it since version 34 of this statement, which an adoption of either kind brings from then on and the Sync run offers a repository that holds the claim protocol alone: a run asked for either, by the control panel’s Tokens page or by an issue, outside crowd mode reads the issue’s comments, so as to say it once, says on the issue, with the repository’s own GitHub token, that the repository does not hold the App’s settings and so stores no token into a pool, and that an owner of the organization adds one with Add Token, and, where an issue started the run, closes that issue as not planned, as a run in crowd mode does too, saying on the issue only that the repository holds no Claude token (the control panel, below). A copy of the whole template made before then keeps the Token workflow it was made with, which neither the Sync run nor the protocol’s releases replace, and where that workflow has those jobs, the store job in a copy made since 00:13 UTC on 2026-10-19 and the manage job too in one made since 02:26 UTC that day, they start there outside crowd mode without the variable, GitHub recording each such run as a deployment to their environment token-store, which it makes in the repository the first time one runs where the repository’s plan lets it have environments, and store and manage nothing: each stops at the first step that needs the App’s token, which in a copy made before 02:26 UTC that day comes after the Claude sign-in, the token then held on the runner and deleted unsaved, and the run then reads the issue’s comments, says on the issue only that it stopped and closes an issue that started it as not planned. The job that makes a token for a page that stores it itself runs there as anywhere (the control panel, below).

SymphonyBoard also asks for one account permission, Codespaces user secrets (read and write), which GitHub asks each person for when they sign in with GitHub on the control panel. The Tokens page used it up to version 13 of this statement to hand its GitHub sign-in to a Codespace; it no longer uses it, and it stays on the App until the developer takes it off.

Symphony Setup asks for two repository permissions, Administration (read and write), for the eight settings below, and Metadata (read), and, on an organization, three organization permissions: Administration (read and write), Secrets (read and write) and Variables (read and write). It uses Administration for one thing only: where the organization holds off “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” for its repositories, as a new organization does, and the repository takes the whole template, the run allows that box for the organization, leaving the default permissions of GitHub Actions’ token as they were, and then ticks it on the repository. With Administration it reads and changes no other setting of the organization. That setting of the organization stays allowed after the run, and repositories the organization makes later inherit it; an owner turns it off under the organization’s Settings, Actions, General, Workflow permissions.

It uses Secrets and Variables for one thing only, lending the person who asked for the adoption their own Claude tokens of the organization’s pool, never one they lent with no say, which only the organization’s owners place, and only where the installation on the organization has them, which GitHub asks an owner of the organization to accept. In the adoption run of one of the organization’s repositories, of either kind, the run first reads, with the Setup App’s own key, its installation on the organization, to make a token with the organization permissions Secrets and Variables (write), which reach every secret and variable of the organization though the run touches only those named here, and the repository permission Metadata (read) on the one repository; the token is kept in a file in the run’s temporary directory and never in its log, and is revoked once the settings are applied or, where GitHub refuses the revocation, which the run does not say, runs out within the hour. With it, before the pull request is opened, the run reads the value of the organization variable SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, which gives each slot’s owner by login and account id, and keeps the slots whose owner is the person who asked by both: the login of the account that opened the request’s issue, compared without case, and that account’s id, which the run takes from the issue. A slot that kept no account id is never lent, since a login passes to whoever takes it once an account is renamed or deleted, and a run given no account id reads none of the organization’s secrets or variables. Nor is a slot ever lent whose settings carry the word organization, a token its owner lent with no say: the run counts it as none of the person’s, reads no record of its secret and names it nowhere, so where the person has no other token in the pool that the run may lend, the pull request says, as below, that no token in it names them as its owner by their login and account id, and the log reads “token lending: no tokens lent”. For each slot it keeps it reads the record of the slot’s organization secret (SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32, and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for the slot main), its name, when it was made and last changed, and whether it is shared with all the organization’s repositories, its private ones or selected ones, never which ones and never its value, which GitHub gives no one, and adds the repository to the repositories that may read it. Where one of those secrets was lent so, or reaches the repository already, shared with all the organization’s repositories or, for a private or internal repository, with its private ones, it does the same for the two variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, whose records hold their values, so it reads the value of SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS, the list of the pool’s slots, and the settings again. The repository’s Claude workflows can then run on those tokens, except in a private repository of an organization on GitHub Free, which GitHub lets read no organization secret or variable, though the run, which reads no plan, lends them all the same and calls them lent or left as they were; and, as with any Actions secret, whoever may write to that repository can have a workflow there use your token or send it elsewhere. It adds a repository only to the list of a secret or a variable that exists and is shared with selected repositories: it changes no visibility, creates nothing and lends no one else’s slot. The two variables’ values stay in the run’s memory. The run’s public log has one line for this, “token lending: tokens lent” or “token lending: no tokens lent”, and says neither which nor how many, nor why none was lent; since only the asker’s own tokens are lent, “tokens lent” does tell anyone who reads it that the person who opened the request holds a token of the organization’s pool and that the installation has the two permissions. The pull request in your repository, which anyone who can read the repository reads, everyone where it is public, names each of your secrets and, where one of them was lent or reaches the repository already, each of the two variables, with what became of it (lent, left as it was, not reaching the repository, missing, or not lent because GitHub refused it or could not be reached, quoting one reason: GitHub’s answer, or the run’s word that GitHub was out of reach, for the first of the two variables not lent, else for the first of your secrets not lent), and says why where none was lent. Where none of the pool’s tokens is yours, it says so with the same hint every time, to press Add Token on the control panel’s Tokens page, so it never says whether a slot names your login. Once the two variables are lent, the settings variable, with every slot owner’s login and account id, reaches the repository too, even where the log says “no tokens lent”, as the section on SymphonyBoard’s pool says of every repository a token is lent to. What is lent stays lent whatever becomes of the pull request, closed without merging or never opened; where the run stops after lending and before it opens the pull request, nothing the run writes names what it lent; where the settings step itself failed after lending, the log reads “token lending: no tokens lent” and the pull request, opened all the same, says only that some settings may be applied and names nothing lent; and where the run is cancelled or runs out of time in that step, its log has no line for the lending. Where the installation has not these two permissions, the run still reads the installation and asks GitHub for the token, lends nothing, and the pull request says your tokens were not lent and where an owner accepts the permissions; for a person’s own repository none of this runs; either way the log reads “token lending: no tokens lent” and the adoption otherwise runs as before. An owner of the organization sees each secret’s and variable’s list, and takes a repository off it, under the organization’s Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, Repository access; a token’s owner may take their own token off a repository from the control panel’s Tokens page, unless they lent it with no say, which they may only delete, as the section on the control panel says.

It has no webhook and receives no event. It is meant to be installed on the repository being adopted. It stays installed after the run, after an adoption or after a request refused because the repository is adopted already, acting only during an adoption run. Its token is made only during a run and revoked when the run’s settings are applied. You can uninstall it at any time from the repository’s or the organization’s Settings, GitHub Apps; the pull request and the run’s answer say so.

In that same run, once GitHub Actions has reported the check, Symphony Setup reads the repository’s own rulesets and writes back the ruleset “Protect the default branch” it created earlier in the run. The only change is GitHub Actions as the source of its required check “check”. It never reads or changes an organization’s ruleset or a ruleset the repository already had.

The adoption

Installing SymphonyBoard sends you on to Symphony Setup’s install page, and that install sends you to a public form on the front door repository, github.com/OpenSpineConsortium/symphony-start. Pressing Create there opens a public issue in your GitHub name; the issue carries what the form held (your installation’s number, or a repository name you typed, the kind, the merge choice and one box) and the run’s answers, and it is closed when the run is done, never deleted. A repository the run learns only by its number is never named on the front door: its name, its owner’s, its default branch’s, your login and your account’s id are masked in the adoption job’s public log after the step that names the repository, whose settings show your login and your account’s id as the issue you opened gives them (the request job’s step that resolves the installation, before it, shows your login too), and the issue is answered with “your repository”. A name you typed into the form is public already, and the run names it in its answers, and its public log shows your login in the settings of the request job’s step that checks you administer it, and your login and your account’s id in the settings of each step of the adoption job from the one that names the repository on. The front door’s public logs do show the installation’s number, the repository’s numeric id, whether the repository belongs to an organization, which the steps of the token lending run for or skip, the kind the run read (whether the repository was empty), how many files it added, replaced, kept or skipped, and the commit ids of your default branch and of the template.

To do its work the run reads, from the repository being adopted: the default branch and the commit on it or, where the default branch is not there yet, whether the repository has any branch at all, whether a branch symphony/adopt exists and has a pull request, whether docs/agents/PROTOCOL.md exists, the one word in .github/symphony-adopt and .github/symphony-metrics and in each under its name before the rename to Symphony, .github/sdlc-adopt and .github/sdlc-metrics, the full listing of the default branch’s tree (to decide the kind), a checkout of that branch at depth one (to add the files) and whether you administer the repository. With Symphony Setup installed, the run also reads the repository’s record, keeping its id, to name it when lending, and its default branch, to limit the environment token-store to it, and whether it is public, private or internal, to say in the pull request whether GitHub enforces its ruleset and, in an organization’s repository, which of the organization’s secrets reach it already; and its rulesets, its topics and its workflow permissions for GitHub Actions, to leave what is there as it is. When the form carries an installation’s number and no name, the run reads that installation’s record and, when the number is Symphony Setup’s, SymphonyBoard’s own list of its installations, to find the one on the same account; then it asks the same of each repository both Apps reach, and whether you administer it, to choose the newest one with no adoption yet. Everything read lives on GitHub’s runner for the length of the run and goes with it; nothing of it is kept or sent elsewhere.

What the run writes to your repository, as the App’s bot: the board’s labels, one commit on the branch symphony/adopt, one pull request from it, and, in a repository that held nothing yet, the issue “Set up this project”. In a repository with no commit at all, the run first makes one, as GitHub’s own “Add a README file” does: a README.md holding the repository’s name, on the default branch, which the pull request goes into; the whole template’s README takes its place when you merge. The pull request’s body lists every file it brings, names the GitHub login of the person who asked, says whether the repository is private and, where the Setup App was installed, quotes GitHub’s own answer for each setting, which may name your account’s plan; in an organization’s new repository, the pull request also writes that login into .github/CODEOWNERS. With Symphony Setup installed, the run creates the default branch’s ruleset, turns on delete-head-branches and auto-merge, adds the topic symphony to the repository’s topics (the sign on the repository’s page that it is adopted, which anyone can see there and the Symphony browser extension reads from the page; your other topics stay), turns on secret scanning and push protection where your plan and visibility allow it, makes the environment token-store, limited to the default branch, unless the repository has an environment of that name, which it leaves as it is (the Token workflow saves a Claude token you lend there with SymphonyBoard’s key, and GitHub would otherwise make the environment on the workflow’s first run open to every branch; where GitHub refuses it, as for a private repository whose plan has no environments, the pull request says so and where to make it, and where it refuses the branch rule after making the environment, the environment stands with no branch allowed, so nothing runs there until you add one), in a repository that takes the whole template ticks “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” where your organization and its enterprise allow it, in an organization’s repository lends it your own Claude tokens of the organization’s pool, but none you lent with no say, and, beside one of them, the pool’s two variables (as the section on what each App asks for says), and, in a repository that takes the whole template, once GitHub Actions has reported the check named “check” on the branch symphony/adopt, sets GitHub Actions as that check’s only source in the ruleset it created, then revokes the Setup App’s token; the Setup App stays installed. Unless you chose on the form to review the pull request first, the run merges it or arms auto-merge. Everything else lands only when you merge. Closing the pull request instead leaves the labels, the README the run made in a repository that had no commit, the branch, the settings, the topic and the issue for you to undo, and, in an organization’s repository, the tokens and the two variables lent to it (as the section on what each App asks for says), which an owner of the organization takes off, as a token’s owner may take their own unless they lent it with no say.

The protocol alone brings, among its files, these workflows: the board’s and the one that tidies a closed issue’s claim branch, the metrics workflow only beside a switch it could write (the section on sharing) and, since version 34 of this statement, the Token workflow, which the control panel’s Tokens page starts to make a Claude token on your repository’s own runner (the section on the control panel) and which every issue opened in your repository starts as well, its jobs skipping unless the issue’s description begins with the line that asks it to lend or manage a token. A workflow that runs a script comes with that script and every module of the template it imports, or not at all: it stays out where anything of yours, a file, a link or a folder, stands where one of them goes, unless it is a file, or a link to a file in the repository outside its .git, that holds the template’s version byte for byte; where a file of yours, or a link of yours to anything but a folder in the repository outside its .git, stands where one of their folders goes; where your repository ignores one of them; where Python would import a file of yours in place of one of them; where one of its modules stays out with another of these workflows that imports it too; or, for the board’s workflow and the metrics workflow, whose scripts import the protocol’s library, which the adoption brings under tools/sdlc_protocol, where that library will not be the template’s once the pull request is merged. The pull request names the file that held it back. Once adopted for the protocol alone, a repository is offered the template’s newer versions of these files by the Sync run (the next section), which offers nothing to a copy of the whole template that keeps its .github/workflows/protocol.yml.

The adoption’s files come from the developer’s private template repository, read with a token that holds Contents read on that one repository and is revoked right after the checkout; only the files in the pull request reach you.

The Sync run

An adoption copies the template’s files once. So that a repository keeps up with the template’s later versions of the files Symphony’s board and the control panel run on, the developer runs a workflow in the template’s own repository, the Sync run (the template’s .github/workflows/sync.yml and tools/sync_adopted.py), whenever the board’s, tidy, metrics, Token or drive sync workflow, scripts/tokens.py or any file under tools/ changes on the template’s default branch, once a week, on Tuesdays at 07:29 UTC, and when someone who may write to the template’s repository starts it by hand. It runs nowhere but there, on GitHub Actions, where SymphonyBoard’s private key is kept: with the key, which it hands to openssl through a pipe and never writes to a file, the run signs the App’s own credential, which lasts less than ten minutes; the template’s own GitHub token there only reads the template. With that credential it reads the App’s own record, for the name its pull requests and commits carry, by which it tells them from anyone else’s, and the list of SymphonyBoard’s installations, the first five thousand where there are more, with the account each is on. For each installation in turn, or, in a run started by hand that names one account, for that account’s alone, it asks GitHub for an installation token with Contents, Pull requests and Workflows (write), Workflows because the files it brings include workflows, which GitHub lets no token write without it, and Metadata (read); reads the list of the repositories that installation reaches, the first five thousand where it reaches more, with the record GitHub gives of each; offers each repository what this section says or, where GitHub fails to give that list whole, offers none of them and counts that installation; and then revokes the token and goes on to the next installation whatever GitHub answers, so a token GitHub did not revoke, which the run does not say, runs out within the hour. An installation for which GitHub answers the request for a token with the status 403, 404 or 422, as it does for a suspended one, is counted and passed over; where GitHub answers that request with any other status from 300 up, with an answer the run cannot read, or not at all, the run stops there, and the installations after it wait for its next run.

It passes over, reading nothing more of it, the template’s and the front door’s own repositories and any repository that is archived, disabled or a fork. Of every other it reads, with that token, the default branch’s newest commit as git records it (its author’s and committer’s names, e-mail addresses and dates, its message, its parents, its signature where it has one and its tree, of which the run uses the tree) and the full listing of that tree: each file’s path, its mode, its size and the id git gives its contents, never the contents. It passes over a repository with no commit, one whose listing GitHub gives cut short, as it does for a very large tree, and one whose default branch holds no file docs/agents/PROTOCOL.md, which every adoption from the front door brings and every copy of the template carries. It then reads, in turn, the text of each of .github/symphony-sync, the Sync run’s own switch, .github/symphony-adopt, the adoption’s, and .github/sdlc-adopt, that switch’s name before the rename to Symphony, that the default branch holds, until one holds the word off, in capitals or not, with nothing beside it but white space (a byte-order mark before it, which the adoption’s own reading of .github/symphony-adopt passes over, keeps it from counting here): such a repository has opted out, and the run does nothing more there, writing nothing and leaving as they are any branch and pull request an earlier offer left. Where none says off, it passes over too, writing nothing there, a repository whose default branch holds .github/workflows/protocol.yml, as every copy of the whole template does unless its owner has removed that workflow, whether the front door adopted the whole template into it or it was made with “Use this template”: such a copy takes the protocol’s releases by that workflow and runs the template’s own tests on these scripts, tests the files alone would leave behind, so the Sync run offers files only to a repository that holds the claim protocol without that workflow, as one adopted for the protocol alone does. A copy of the whole template made since the template holds the Sync run carries .github/workflows/sync.yml too, whose runs there skip its one job, so nothing of the Sync run runs outside the template’s own repository. It reads no other file of yours, beyond the lines of changed files that GitHub’s comparison of your default branch with the branch symphony/sync shows (below): it compares your files with the template’s by the ids in the listing alone.

What it offers comes in units, as the adoption of the protocol alone brings them: the vendored library with its record (tools/sdlc_protocol and tools/VENDORED), the board’s workflow with its script, the workflow that tidies closed claims, the metrics workflow with the scripts it runs, the Token workflow with the scripts it runs and the drive sync’s workflow, .github/workflows/drive-sync.yml, with the scripts it runs, each script with every module of the template it imports and every one it loads by its path, as the metrics workflow’s tools/usage.py loads tools/profile.py, all as the template holds them at its newest commit. A unit is offered whole or not at all. A file of yours is replaced only where it holds, by that id, a version that some commit in the history of the template’s default branch, the commits of each branch merged into it among them, has held at that path; where one of a unit’s files is anything else, a file of your own, a link, a submodule or a folder, where a file, a link or a submodule of yours stands where a folder of the unit’s goes, or where Python would import a file of yours in place of one of the unit’s modules, the unit is held back, and a pull request the run opens or writes anew for the other units names that file. Whether your default branch has a unit is read from one file of it alone, the unit’s workflow or, for the library, tools/VENDORED. A unit your default branch does not have is not added, since you removed it or never took it, with two exceptions, the Token workflow and the drive sync’s workflow, each with its scripts, which are added where they are missing (the drive sync’s runs nothing on its schedule until Track, or the Folders tab opening a repository that tracks a drive already, has set the repository’s variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE, below, and reads no drive until a drive’s token is there); a unit you have gains every file of it that your default branch lacks, whether a module its newer scripts import or load by its path, a file the newer library holds that yours does not, a script or module of the unit you deleted while keeping its workflow or, where tools/VENDORED stands without tools/sdlc_protocol, the whole library. So the metrics workflow, which shares aggregates, is offered only to a repository that has it already, whose switch .github/symphony-metrics still decides whether anything is shared (the section on sharing). A unit whose scripts import the library is offered only where the library is the template’s already or comes in the same pull request, and the library is held back where a unit that imports it is. Where nothing needs changing, or every unit that would change is held back, the run writes nothing: it opens no pull request, names no file and leaves as it is any pull request an earlier run opened.

Where something does, it works out one value from the files it would bring, each one’s path with the mode and the id git gives the template’s version of it, and reads the twenty newest pull requests from the branch symphony/sync, with the record GitHub gives of each (its title, its description, its author, its state and its two branches among them). Of these it uses only those SymphonyBoard opened into your default branch: whether each is open, the number and the description of the open one or, where none is open, the description of the newest, and whether that newest one was merged. Where none of them is open and the newest was closed without its merge and its description holds that same value, as it does where that pull request offered those same files, each at the same version, it stops there, writing nothing. Otherwise it reads whether the branch symphony/sync exists and, where it does, GitHub’s comparison of your default branch with it, which gives the records of your default branch’s newest commit, of the newest commit the two share and of every commit the branch holds beyond your default branch, as many as GitHub lists in one answer, each with its author’s and committer’s names, e-mail addresses, dates and accounts, its message, its signature where it has one, its tree and its parents; how many such commits there are; and the files the branch changes since the commit the two share, with lines of each change. Of it the run uses how many commits the branch holds beyond your default branch and, of each one listed, its author’s account and how many parents it has. Where one of those commits is neither SymphonyBoard’s, by its author’s account, nor a merge, because someone pushed a commit of their own to the branch, or where the branch holds more of them than GitHub lists, the run leaves the branch and any pull request from it as they are, writing nothing, and offers that repository nothing more while the branch holds such a commit, or more commits than GitHub lists, beyond your default branch. A merge made on the branch, such as GitHub’s Update branch makes, holds nothing back by itself, whoever made it, and the run’s next offer drops it from the branch with whatever it brought; but a commit the merge brought in that your default branch does not hold is one of the commits the branch holds beyond your default branch, so where such a commit is neither SymphonyBoard’s nor a merge, as a commit of another branch of yours merged in may be, the run leaves the branch and any pull request from it as they are, as it does for a commit pushed to the branch. Where the branch exists and one of SymphonyBoard’s pull requests from it is open and its description holds that same value, the run also reads the branch’s newest commit as git records it (its author’s and committer’s names, e-mail addresses and dates, its message, its parents, its signature where it has one and its tree, of which the run uses the parents), and it stops there, writing nothing, where that commit stands straight on your default branch’s newest commit, its one parent, as the run’s own commit does. Otherwise it writes, as SymphonyBoard, each file it brings as a git object in your repository, a file that is not UTF-8 text in a call of its own and the rest in the call that writes the tree; one tree, your default branch’s tree with those files in place; and one commit, whose message is “Bring Symphony’s board files up to date” followed by a blank line and the line “Offered by the Symphony template’s sync.”, on your default branch’s newest commit, with SymphonyBoard as its author and committer. It sets the branch symphony/sync to that commit, making the branch or moving it by force, so the branch holds the newest offer alone and an earlier offer’s commit, and any merge made on the branch, is dropped from it. It then opens one pull request from that branch into your default branch, titled “Bring Symphony’s board files up to date”, or, where one SymphonyBoard opened from that branch into your default branch is open already, writes that pull request’s description anew. Where GitHub refuses to open it, as it does while a pull request someone else opened from that branch into your default branch stands open, the branch keeps the commit the run moved it to, with no pull request of SymphonyBoard’s from it, and the repository is counted refused; and since no open pull request of SymphonyBoard’s then holds that value, each later run that gets this far writes the offer again, as a new commit on your default branch’s newest commit, moves the branch to it by force and asks again to open the pull request, so that the other pull request shows each move, with the offer as its changes. The description lists every file the pull request brings, names each unit held back and why, by the file of yours that held it or, for the library and a unit that imports it, by the unit or the library it waits on, says how to stop the offers, and begins with a hidden line holding the value worked out from the files offered, a digest (SHA-256) of each one’s path with the mode and the id git gives the template’s version of it. So a pull request you close without merging is not offered again while the files it would bring, each at the template’s version, stay the same, whatever else changes on your default branch; once they differ, because the template changed, added or dropped one of them or because a change on your default branch makes one of them current, holds a unit back or lets one through, the next run offers them again, in a new pull request. An open one is built again whenever a run finds the files offered changed, that hidden line gone from its description, or the branch’s newest commit anything but one commit straight on your default branch’s newest commit, as it is once anything is committed to your default branch or a merge is made on the branch: the run then writes the offer again on your default branch’s newest commit, moves the branch to it and writes the description anew. Where a call fails, or the run stops, after the run has written the files, the tree or the commit and before the branch symphony/sync points to that commit, as one fails where a rule of your repository refuses SymphonyBoard the branch, the objects it wrote stay in your repository’s storage with no branch pointing to them, holding the template’s files, your own tree’s listing with those files in place and, where it got that far, the commit described above, with its message, SymphonyBoard as its author and committer and your default branch’s newest commit as its parent, and nothing else.

Like any branch and pull request an App makes, and as the adoption’s do, the branch and the pull request start, on your repository’s own token and Actions allowance, the workflows your repository runs on a push, a new branch or a pull request, the offered ones among them, each in the version the branch holds, save one that runs on pull_request_target, which GitHub runs in your default branch’s version. Nothing on your default branch changes until you merge the pull request. The run keeps nothing it reads beyond the run, holding it in its memory on GitHub’s runner, sends nothing anywhere but GitHub’s API, and the developer’s collector receives nothing from it. Its log, which whoever may read the template’s repository can read, every member of the developer’s enterprise while the template is internal, says only how many repositories met each outcome (offered, updated, offered already, up to date, declined, opted out, not adopted, whole template, for a repository that holds .github/workflows/protocol.yml and is offered nothing, skipped, branch theirs, refused, for a call GitHub answered with a status from 400 to 499 other than 429, and failed), for how many installations GitHub gave no token and for how many it failed to give the list of the repositories they reach, with those two counts and the count refused repeated as warnings on the run’s page, or, where the run stops, in place of all those counts, the method of the call GitHub refused and the status it answered with or, where GitHub gave no answer or one the run could not read, or something else stopped it, the error Python met, with the lines of code, the run’s own and Python’s, where it met it; it names no repository, account or file, save that a run started by hand for one account shows that account’s login as whoever started it typed it. A repository where a call fails is counted and the run goes on to the next, starting that one over in its next run. Uninstalling SymphonyBoard stops the Sync run’s reads and offers, and so does taking a repository off the installation’s list, for that repository; an offer’s branch and pull request stay until you close and delete them.

Field metrics: what the developer receives

A repository Symphony set up runs its own workflow once a day, with GitHub’s own token, which writes one file, METRICS.json, to a branch named metrics of your repository: eleven counts (claims, pull requests opened, merged, closed unmerged, reviews, changes requested, check runs passed and failed, conflicts seen, released claims, contributors), the median and 90th percentile of three waits in seconds, two rates, the time it was made, the number of days it covers (30), the protocol’s release number and the short id of its commit, and the words that name the schema and the switch. Since version 2 of this statement the file also holds counts of how the work ran in parallel, so that failure can be compared between one person running several Claude Code sessions at once and several people working at once: seventeen counts of the people who opened pull requests, the Claude Code sessions named on them, how many named one, the most pull requests, people and sessions of one person at work at the same moment, the conflicts the board marked or GitHub reports on open pull requests, and the pull requests the run could not read in full; for each of eight work settings (nothing else at work beside it; one session’s several pull requests; one person’s several sessions; several people; several people beside one person’s several sessions; not known; the repository’s own Claude workflows; other apps and bots), thirteen counts and sums for the pull requests that ended in the 30 days and those still open, such as how many merged, met a conflict or shared a changed file with work beside them, and how long they were at work; and, for four kinds of pairs of pull requests at work at the same time, seven counts of how many pairs there were and how many worked at once, shared a file, had one land while the other was open, or met in conflict when it did. Since version 3 it also holds what the work cost, so that the cost of coordination can be measured: the date of the price list the estimate uses; counts of the pull requests that ended in the 30 days, of those merged and of those with any usage recorded against them, of the Claude Code sessions and the runs of the repository’s Claude workflows that recorded usage, and of the records left for a later run; the tokens Claude used, by kind (input, cache writes, cache reads, output, in all, and those of a model the price list does not know) and by model family (the fixed words fable, opus, sonnet, haiku and other, never a model’s name); what those tokens would cost at Anthropic’s API list prices, in dollars, and the part of it the coordinator workflow spent; the seconds Claude was at work; the commits, failed checks and reverts of those pull requests; four of these per merged pull request; and, for the pull requests done alone and those done with other work beside them, thirteen counts and sums each (pull requests, merged, measured, measured and merged, tokens, dollars, seconds, commits, failed checks, first checks passed and judged, the median wait from opening to merge, and the time at work), with seven ratios between the two. To make the file the workflow reads from GitHub’s API, in its memory only and for the length of the run, the pull requests changed in the 30 days and in the 30 before them, their commits, reviews, check runs and changed files, the comments made or edited on the repository’s issues and pull requests in those 60 days, its branches and, for each claim branch with no pull request changed in the 30 days, its newest commit; to sort the pull requests it uses the login of the person who opened each one, the name of its branch, the Claude Code session link a cloud session writes into its commit messages and pull request descriptions (and a line Symphony-Session: where a session writes one) and the times of its commits, and to see whose files meet, the names of the files each changed; it writes none of them. For what the work cost it reads two records the template’s own tools leave in your repository, never anything from the App: the line Symphony-Usage: that a Claude Code session of the repository adds to each of its commit messages, holding token counts by model, the seconds the session was at work and the first eight characters of the session’s id, and no word of its conversation; and the usage record each run of the repository’s Claude workflows keeps as an artifact of that run, holding token counts by model, seconds, turns, the workflow, the job and the worker’s name, and the issue and pull request the run was for, and nothing of the conversation. It lists and downloads those artifacts with the repository’s own token, from the last 60 days, and keeps the records it has read in the repository’s own Actions cache, so the next day’s run reads only the new ones. The file holds no name, login, session link or session id, title, branch name, file name, link, issue number, model name, worker name, text or code; a test in the template fails if any of those reaches the file. Where a repository has few pull requests a count can describe a single one, and the counts say how a project works, for instance that one person had three sessions’ work going at once. The branch is as visible as your repository. A maintainer of your project who chooses to run the template’s judge on their own computer, with their own Claude Code account, adds a second file, JUDGE.json, holding counts of communication failure types, of the conversations it judged and of those that had two or more people, in all and for each work setting, the totals of the failure types’ three groups, the number of pull requests it covered that ended in the 30 days, in each work setting, the number of days it covered and any limit it ran under, the time it was made, which model and which version of its prompt it used, and the word that names its schema; the App never runs that judge and only reads that file.

Once a day, at 04:17 UTC, the developer’s collector lists the repositories every installation of SymphonyBoard reaches (receiving from GitHub their names, owners and visibility, which it holds in memory and never writes) and asks each for exactly those two files at the ref metrics, and for no other path. It keeps a project’s METRICS.json only when the file says sharing is on; otherwise nothing of that project is stored and JUDGE.json is not read. Of each file it keeps a fixed list of numbers, the time the file was made, the date of the price list and the few identifier-shaped words named above; a value of another shape is dropped. The names of the work settings, of the kinds of pairs, of the model families and of the two sides of the comparison are fixed words of the template, the same in every repository’s file, never words of your project. The developer therefore learns, per repository and day, how the protocol performed in numbers, and nothing of what the work was.

Each kept line names the repository only as a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256) of its GitHub node id under a secret the developer alone holds, derived from the App’s private key or set separately, so the developer can follow one repository’s numbers from day to day, and across a rename or transfer, without the dataset naming it; a reader of the dataset without that secret cannot tell which repository a line is. Rotating the key or the secret gives every repository a new hash and ends the thread. The dataset is a private branch of the developer’s repository, one JSON line per repository and day, with no expiry: lines are added beside earlier days’, a second run on the same day replaces that day’s, and the branch’s git history keeps every earlier version for as long as the branch exists. It is read by the developer and by the collaborators on that private repository, for research on how coordination fails and succeeds among Claude Code sessions; it is never sold and never given to anyone else. The developer runs the collector on GitHub Actions; it talks to api.github.com and nowhere else.

Sharing is on by default, with three ways off

Sharing is on unless you turn it off: the adoption writes on into .github/symphony-metrics unless you ticked the form’s box “Do not share anonymous aggregates” or a switch of the repository’s own says off already, under that name or under .github/sdlc-metrics, its name before the rename to Symphony, which the adoption never turns on. Where the switch cannot be written, because the repository ignores it or something of its own stands where it goes, nothing the adoption brings shares: the protocol alone then brings no metrics workflow, and the whole template’s reads what stands in the switch’s place as off. To turn it off at any time: write off as the first word of .github/symphony-metrics on your default branch (in a repository adopted before the rename, whose workflow reads only .github/sdlc-metrics, write it there), or set the repository Actions variable SDLC_METRICS to off (and run the workflow once, so the record on the branch says off), or uninstall SymphonyBoard, after which the collector reaches nothing of yours. Disabling the workflow alone does not stop sharing, because the branch keeps its last record and the collector reads it as that day’s; turn the switch off first. With the switch off the template’s sessions also stop adding the Symphony-Usage: line to their commits and its Claude workflows stop keeping usage records, and a person who wants no usage of theirs on their commits whatever the repository says sets SDLC_METRICS to off in their own environment. Lines already collected stay in the dataset under the hash; they carry nothing that names you.

The control panel

The control panel is a page of the developer’s site, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/, and the cost page beside it, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/cost.html. Both are static files that work in your browser with a GitHub token you give them, and they talk to GitHub’s own API as you and, only when you sign in with GitHub or open the Folders tab, to the sign-in service described below, and, for a drive you connect there, to Microsoft (the Folders tab, below); and each time your browser loads either of them, the control panel as the installed app (below) among them, the page links the site’s typefaces from Google Fonts, which your browser asks Google for (below). They read your own account’s login (to say who is signed in), your repository’s board (the file STATE.md on the branch board), its open issues and their labels, for its Dependencies tab (below) the sub-issues of each open issue labelled epic or goal and the issues blocking each of an epic’s sub-issues, the worker files under .github/symphony/workers/, the agents’ list .github/symphony/agents.json and the agent files under .claude/agents/ it names, for an agent’s tokens the file .github/symphony/accounts.json, which names the token slots each agent may use, and the default branch’s tools/pool.py, to see that it takes such a list before one is proposed, on the Tokens page the records on the branch pool of each slot’s latest use (how much of its five-hour and seven-day windows, and of any weekly limit of a single model, named by that model, it had used, when they reset, for a reading taken from a worker’s run or a probe whether Claude’s answer it was read from allowed or refused the request, and when and by what it was read), its open pull requests and the check runs on their heads, its Actions runs, the repository’s own record (its default branch, whether it is private, its topics and, for one you name, its numeric id and its owner’s, to build the App’s install link with that repository selected), on the cost page the file METRICS.json on the branch metrics, and, when you press “Find my Symphony repositories”, the names and topics of the repositories your token reaches, up to three hundred of the most recently pushed, to keep the ones carrying the topic symphony, and, in the dialog “Add repository”, the repositories SymphonyBoard is installed on that you can reach, installation by installation, or, with a pasted token, the repositories that token reaches, to choose one to add to your list; on the Share tab, who has access to the repository (its direct collaborators in an organization’s repository, all of them in a person’s) with their roles, the invitations waiting for an answer and, among its open issues, the requests to join, each an issue whose description begins with the line <!-- symphony-access: request -->, one row for each person who asked; and, before it opens a request to join for you, your own open issues there, so that it opens no second one. On the Tokens page they also read, as you, the names and records of the organization’s Actions secrets (for a personal account’s repository, the repository’s own), never a value, which GitHub gives no one, to show which slots hold a token and to find a free one; the name and value of every Actions variable there, read to find each slot’s label, of which the page keeps the labels alone; the variable SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS and, for an owner of the organization, SYMPHONY_LEND_TO; and, when you press Add Token, the variable CLAUDE_CROWD of the organization and of the repository, to refuse a repository in crowd mode. Only when you press the button that says so, they write what GitHub’s own pages would: an issue (a task, an “Add a worker” issue, one that mentions @claude, the assistant’s, below, or a request to join, which the page opens as you, titled “Access request:” and your login, with a description that names your login and the repository and says that you ask to join it as a collaborator, when you press “Ask to join” on the Share tab of a repository where GitHub will not show you who has access, or in the Tokens page’s Add dialog for an organization’s repository you may not write to, and which anyone who can read the repository can read, everyone where it is public), a comment (a question to the assistant among them, and, on a request to join that someone answers on the Share tab, with Invite, which only an administrator may, or with its X to decline and confirm, which anyone GitHub shows the repository’s collaborators to may, every collaborator in a person’s repository and, in an organization’s, a member of the organization who may write to it, one saying that they invited you, that you have access already or, whoever declined, that an administrator declined), a label on an issue (and the label itself when it is not there yet), a workflow run started by hand, a merge, an issue closed as not planned or, for a request to join answered with Invite, as completed, a pull request closed, a pull request that changes or deletes a worker’s file or deletes an agent’s file and its line in agents.json, made as GitHub’s own pages would make it (a branch of its own from the default branch’s head, the files written or deleted on that branch, and the pull request opened, or the one already open from that branch found), never a push to the default branch, a pull request from the Agents tab that gives an agent the token slots you picked, by their names in .github/symphony/accounts.json, written on the branch symphony/tokens-<the agent’s name in lower case>, which is first set to the default branch’s head, so whatever that branch held is replaced, and set to merge itself once its checks pass where the repository allows auto-merge (the Notebooks tab, below, writes a file too, and makes a notebook’s repository private when you ask), or, on the Share tab, an invitation to the GitHub user you name, with the role you pick, or, when you answer their request to join with Invite, to the person who asked, with Write in an organization’s repository and a collaborator’s access in a person’s, to collaborate on the repository, a new role for a collaborator or for an invitation waiting, a collaborator removed or an invitation withdrawn (the Folders tab, below, says what else). To find that user from an email address you type, the Share tab asks GitHub’s user search for an account showing that address publicly; the address goes to GitHub alone. The Share tab’s mail buttons open Gmail, Outlook, your email app or your device’s share sheet with a note you send yourself; the page sends nothing there.

The token is one of two kinds, and either way it stays in your browser. A fine-grained personal access token you make on GitHub and paste into the page is first sent to GitHub alone, to ask whose it is, and kept only once GitHub accepts it: in the browser’s storage until you press “Forget the token”, or, when you did not tick “Keep me signed in”, in the tab’s own storage, which the browser clears when the tab closes and brings back with the tab when it reopens or restores it. With “Sign in with GitHub”, GitHub issues, after you allow it on GitHub’s own page, a token of SymphonyBoard’s that acts as you within the App’s permissions and your own access on the repositories it is installed on, and expires in eight hours; beside it GitHub issues a refresh token, valid six months, with which the page renews the token. Pressed in a browser’s tab, “Sign in with GitHub” first keeps in the tab’s own storage a one-time value, a one-time secret it made for this sign-in, whether “Keep me signed in” is ticked and the page’s query (the repository it showed), then leaves for GitHub’s page, sending GitHub that value and a hash of the secret, and GitHub sends your browser back to the page with a one-time code and the same value (the installed app, below, is another matter); on that return the page takes the code out of its address, forgets what it kept, puts its query back and, where the value matches, sends the code, with the one-time secret, to the sign-in service, a small program of the developer’s run on Cloudflare’s Workers platform, which adds the App’s client secret, asks GitHub for the token and hands back the token and the refresh token; the page renews the token by sending the service the refresh token the same way. What it kept for a sign-in that never comes back stays in the tab’s own storage, which “Forget the token” does not clear, until another press of “Sign in with GitHub” replaces it, a return from GitHub or from Microsoft (the Folders tab, below) reaches that tab, or the browser clears the tab’s own storage, as above. With “Keep me signed in” ticked, the page keeps both in the browser’s storage until you press “Forget the token”. Unticked, it keeps the token in the tab’s own storage, as it keeps a pasted token, and the refresh token in the open page’s memory alone, never in the browser’s storage, so that the renewals end once that page is gone, closed, reloaded or replaced by another page such as the cost page, and the sign-in then ends with its eight-hour token. When a new sign-in, or a token you paste that GitHub accepts, takes the place of a sign-in’s token, the page has the service ask GitHub to revoke the one it replaced, as “Forget the token” does. The service keeps nothing: no store, no cookie, and no log of its own of the code, the tokens or you; it answers no origin but the site’s (the Folders tab, below, says what else); and its host’s own request logs are turned off, though Cloudflare, which carries the request, sees its address and timing under Cloudflare’s own privacy policy. The developer receives nothing from the pages but what that service passes through in the moment: never a token to keep, never a name, never a count. Beside the token, the page keeps in your browser the names of the repositories you listed, the plan you chose on the cost page, the number of the assistant issue it uses in each repository (below), which chart you last chose on each repository’s Dependencies tab, by the repository’s name and the chart’s (below), and the layout you set: the widths and heights of the panels you resized and the text size, numbers alone, holding nothing of your repositories or of GitHub and sent nowhere.

The control panel can also be installed from the browser as an app, on a phone’s Home Screen or among a computer’s apps; its manifest is https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/manifest.webmanifest. The app is the same page in a window of its own, with no code of its own: it reads, sends and keeps what the page does, as this section says, its window standing for the tab, save for its sign-in. While sign-in by code, below, is switched off, the app’s “Sign in with GitHub” leaves for GitHub’s page as a tab’s does, but GitHub’s return may land in your browser rather than in the app. The page there did not start that sign-in and holds no secret for it, so it takes the code out of its address and sends it nowhere, and the code signs nobody in; the app is then not signed in by that press, and its window keeps what the press kept, the one-time value and secret, the tick and the page’s query, in its own storage, as a tab keeps them (above), until another press of “Sign in with GitHub” replaces them, a return from GitHub or from Microsoft reaches the app, or that storage is cleared as a tab’s is. The way in is then a token pasted into the app or, where the app shares its browser’s storage with that browser’s tabs, as some browsers’ installed apps do, a sign-in or a token kept on that browser with “Keep me signed in” ticked, which the app reads as it opens, as a tab does. There what the app keeps with that box ticked the browser’s tabs read too, and the app’s “Forget the token” forgets what that browser keeps, for its tabs as for the app, though not a sign-in a tab holds for itself alone, and has the service ask GitHub to revoke a sign-in’s token among it, as a tab’s does.

Each time your browser loads the control panel, in a tab or as the installed app, or the cost page, the page’s head, as on the developer’s site’s other Symphony pages, links a stylesheet of Google Fonts, https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2, asking for three typefaces: Newsreader (upright at the weights 400, 500 and 600 and italic at 400 and 500, across its optical sizes 6 to 72), IBM Plex Sans (400, 500 and 600) and IBM Plex Mono (400 and 500); and it asks the browser to open a connection to fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com as it loads. Your browser asks fonts.googleapis.com for that stylesheet and fonts.gstatic.com for the font files it names, as the page’s text comes to need them, unless it holds them from an earlier load. Google receives those requests as it receives any, with your network address and the headers your browser sends with every request, under Google’s own privacy policy, and the request for the stylesheet names the page it came from as browsers do unless set otherwise, by the site’s address alone, https://openspineconsortium.com/, and not by the page’s own address, whose query can name a repository, while each request for a font file, which browsers fetch as a cross-origin request, names the site too, by its origin, https://openspineconsortium.com, and names the stylesheet that asked for it by Google’s own address alone, https://fonts.googleapis.com/, as browsers do unless set otherwise; the page puts nothing of its own into them, no token, no repository’s name and nothing you type, and the developer receives nothing of them.

Sign-in by code, GitHub’s device flow, is built into both pages for the installed app and switched off: a setting in the page’s script, CODE_SIGNIN, holds it off until the developer turns it on, and while it is off no page offers a code and the page never asks the sign-in service for one. GitHub gives a SymphonyBoard code only while “Enable Device Flow” is ticked in the App’s settings, which the developer ticks only to turn sign-in by code on. Once it is on, the installed app’s “Sign in with GitHub” signs in by code in place of leaving for GitHub’s page, and in a browser’s tab a second button beside it, “Sign in with a code instead”, does the same. On that press the page sends the sign-in service’s route /device a request that holds nothing of yours, an empty object, which your browser sends with the page’s origin; the service asks GitHub, at https://github.com/login/device/code, for a code, with SymphonyBoard’s client id alone, which is public, and no client secret, and hands back the short code you type, the address of GitHub’s page where you type it, the device code that goes with it, how long the two live, an hour at most, and how often the page may ask after them. The page shows the short code, with the warning below, and holds the device code in the open page’s memory alone, never in the browser’s storage, the page’s address or a log. The link beside the code, “Copy it and open GitHub”, puts the short code on your device’s clipboard and opens https://github.com/login/device in a new tab, handing that page nothing; you type the code there, where GitHub names SymphonyBoard and asks whether it may act as you. Meanwhile the page sends the device code alone to the service’s route /device/token, at most once every five seconds and more slowly where GitHub or the service asks, and the service passes it to GitHub, at https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token, with the client id and no client secret, and hands back GitHub’s word that the code is not typed yet or that the page should ask more slowly, GitHub’s refusal, its own word that GitHub could not be reached or answered with trouble of the moment, a server error or a limit with no word of its own, on which the page asks again at the same pace, as it does when the service itself cannot be reached or gives no answer the page can read, or, once you have typed it and allowed SymphonyBoard, the token and the refresh token, the same kinds the sign-in by GitHub’s page gives, which the page renews and revokes through the service in the same way. The page stops asking when GitHub gives the token or refuses, when the service refuses the request or fails at it, save at its limit on one address’s calls, on which the page asks more slowly, when the code runs out, or when you press Cancel, sign in another way, paste a token GitHub accepts or press “Forget the token”; a token GitHub gives after that, for a code the page has let go of, goes once more to the service, so that GitHub revokes it. Once you are signed in by code, the page keeps what the sign-in by GitHub’s page keeps, as above, by “Keep me signed in” as it stands when the token comes: ticked, the token and the refresh token in the browser’s storage until you press “Forget the token”; unticked, the token in the tab’s own storage and the refresh token in the open page’s memory alone. Save where the browser refuses to store the token, as it can for a sign-in by code, which, unlike the sign-in by GitHub’s page, needs no storage to finish: the page then holds the token in the open page’s memory alone, and the refresh token there too where “Keep me signed in” is unticked and nowhere where it is ticked, never renews them, and drops them once that page is gone, you press “Forget the token”, or a sign-in by code or a token you paste that GitHub accepts takes their place, none of which in that case asks GitHub to revoke that token, so the token stays good at GitHub until it runs out within eight hours, or until Revoke at https://github.com/settings/apps/authorizations, below, ends it. The service keeps nothing of a sign-in by code either: no store, no cookie and no log of its own, and its two device routes answer the site’s origin alone.

Ticking “Enable Device Flow” opens a way in that no page can close: anyone, not only this page, may then ask GitHub for a SymphonyBoard code with the App’s public client id, and whoever asked for a code gets the token it earns once a person types it on GitHub’s page and allows SymphonyBoard there, a page that names SymphonyBoard alike for every code. A person talked into typing someone else’s code so hands that someone a token that acts as them, within SymphonyBoard’s permissions and their own access, on every repository the App is installed on that they can reach. So beside every code it shows, the page says: “Type a code only there, on github.com/login/device, and only one you started on this page a moment ago. A code someone sends you, by mail, chat or another page, would sign them in as you.” The developer never sends anyone a code. And whoever holds the refresh token of a sign-in by code can keep that sign-in going without end: GitHub renews such a refresh token with the client id alone, with no client secret and without the sign-in service, each renewal giving a new refresh token good for six months more, so the sign-in ends only when it is revoked or goes six months without a renewal. “Forget the token” drops the token and the refresh token that tab and that browser hold and asks GitHub, through the service, to revoke each sign-in’s token that the tab’s own storage or the browser’s storage holds, which can be two, and no other, so not one the browser refused to store; whether GitHub then refuses such a sign-in’s refresh token too is not established, though the page no longer holds it. Revoke beside SymphonyBoard under your GitHub Settings, Applications, Authorized GitHub Apps, https://github.com/settings/apps/authorizations, ends every token and refresh token GitHub has issued SymphonyBoard for you, one from a code someone else started among them.

The control panel’s Assistant section asks the repository’s own Claude workflow a question, through GitHub and nothing else. Once per repository and person, on your press, the page opens an issue of yours titled Assistant: <your login> and labelled assistant, and makes that label when the repository lacks it; each question you press Ask on is one comment of yours on that issue, which mentions @claude and ends with a short block of the page’s state (the repository’s name, the task the page centres, the filter it shows and the board section it is at), and the repository’s Claude workflow answers it there, on the Claude token the repository holds, reading the repository only, as a comment the page shows you. While it waits, the page reads that issue’s comments every few seconds, then every half minute, for at most forty-five minutes or until you press “Stop watching”, each read made conditional on the last so that GitHub answers “nothing new” at no cost against your rate limit. The page offers the box only where GitHub, asked, says you may write to the repository, since the workflow answers nobody else, and only where the repository’s default branch carries the assistant’s file, .github/symphony/assistant.md, which the page reads to tell. The number of the assistant issue it uses in each repository, one it opened or found, is kept in your browser beside the token, so that it opens no second one; close the issue on GitHub and the page opens another at your next question. The question, its block and the answer are on the issue, where GitHub keeps them as it keeps any issue’s comments, and are sent to nobody else: the developer receives none of it.

The bar’s button “Ask in claude.ai” opens claude.ai in a new browser tab, signed in as whoever you are there, with your question and a line or two naming what the page shows (the repository and the tab, and the task, the OneDrive folder and item or the words of a search of your drive, or the Explore level you are at, each with its GitHub or OneDrive link) carried in that tab’s address, as the question claude.ai starts with. The page itself sends nothing to claude.ai, reads nothing from it and writes nothing for it, asks no write access to the repository for it, and cuts the whole to 2,000 characters, which an address carries. What you and Claude do there is on your own claude.ai account, under Anthropic’s terms, with whatever you connected to that account; the developer receives none of it.

The control panel’s Dependencies tab, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/#dependencies, draws the work of each open epic as a chart: its tasks, which are the epic’s sub-issues on GitHub, an arrow from each issue that blocks one of them to the issue it blocks, which is GitHub’s own blocked-by relation, and the goals above their epics, the chart the repository’s own board draws into STATE.md once its protocol is new enough to draw it. To draw it the page reads, as you, with the GitHub token you gave it, what GitHub’s own issue pages show under Sub-issues and Relationships: the sub-issues of each open issue labelled epic or goal, unless GitHub’s summary of that issue says it has none, and, for each sub-issue of an epic whose summary counts an issue blocking it, the issues blocking it. It makes these reads whenever it reads the repository’s open issues, which it does each time it opens a repository, when you press Refresh, and after you queue a task, give an issue to a worker, mention @claude or merge a pull request on the page, whether or not the Dependencies tab is open, and never on a timer of its own; it makes at most sixty for one drawing, each page of a list counting as one, and none once GitHub says your token has fewer than a hundred calls left in its hour.
