GitHub answers each read with the issues it names as its API describes any issue, and the page keeps for the chart their number, title, state, labels and link, the counts GitHub’s two summaries give for each (its sub-issues, done and in all, and the issues blocking it, open and in all), and which of them an open pull request from its claim branch in the repository itself names, from the pull requests the page already shows; it reads whether each is a pull request and which repository it belongs to, to leave out pull requests and the issues of another repository, and keeps nothing else, in the open page’s memory alone, until it draws again or the page is gone. The chart is drawn in your browser by a copy of Mermaid, an open-source drawing library (MIT) that the developer’s site carries and the page loads from the site, as it loads its own files, only when there is a chart to draw, and the Board tab draws the same way the charts the board’s own STATE.md holds, which the page already reads, each only where every line of it is one the board writes, showing any other block there as text and never drawing it; beside the drawing library’s file from the developer’s site, and the site’s typefaces from Google Fonts, which the page asks for as its text needs them (above), the tab asks nothing of anyone but GitHub. Pressing a node, here or in the Board tab, or a row’s “Centre its row”, opens the Tasks tab at that task’s row, where the task tables hold it, and asks GitHub nothing; that task is then the one the page centres, which the assistant’s next question names, as above. The tab writes nothing to GitHub, whose issues it only reads. Where it has two charts or more, a row of tiles above them, All, Goals and one for each epic, shows one chart at a time, or every one for All, and when you press a tile, with the mouse or the arrow keys, or step to the chart beside it with Previous or Next, the page keeps in your browser’s storage which chart you chose for that repository, by the repository’s name, its owner’s with it, and the chart’s, every chart, the goals or the epic’s number, so that the tab opens on that chart again the next time it draws that repository’s charts while that chart is still among them; it sends that nowhere and keeps it until you choose another chart in that repository, and neither “Forget the token” nor taking the repository off your list removes it. The chart itself is gone with the page, and the developer receives none of it.

The control panel’s Explore tab, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/#explore, shows the same work as a map you go into one level at a time: the repository, its goals and epics, each epic’s tasks, a task’s open pull requests (or, where it has none, its claim branch), the GitHub Actions runs on that branch, each run’s jobs and steps and, at the bottom, the lines of a job’s log, cut to one step’s lines by the times GitHub gives each step. Down to the tasks it draws only what the page has already read, as above, and makes no read of its own. Below a task it reads, as you, with the GitHub token you gave it, only when you go into a level and once for each: the runs on that branch (the latest twenty), a run’s jobs and their steps, and a job’s log, which GitHub hands over from its own storage, the address GitHub’s answer names, and your browser asks that storage for the log with no token of yours, since a browser drops the token when GitHub sends it elsewhere; where your browser may not read it from there, the tab says so and links the log on GitHub. It reads none of these once GitHub says your token has fewer than a hundred calls left in its hour. A job’s log is what GitHub shows anyone who may read the repository’s Actions, and it may hold whatever the job printed, a Claude run’s conversation among it. The tab keeps what it reads in the open page’s memory alone, the lines of the last three jobs’ logs you opened and no more, until you choose another repository or the page is gone, and reads a level again only when you press Read again; it writes nothing, not to GitHub and not to your browser’s storage, and the developer receives none of it.

The control panel’s Notebooks tab, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/#notebooks, shows the notebooks the drive organizer proposes for a private repository (not public, and not internal, which every member of its enterprise can read): groups of a few of your drive’s files, each meant to become a private repository of its own that points at those files where they are and never moves them. It reads, as you, with the GitHub token you gave it, two files on the repository’s branch drive-catalog: notebooks.json, the proposal (each notebook’s title, summary, repository name and the paths of its files), and catalog.json, the names, kinds, sizes, dates and OneDrive links of the drive’s files, as the drive organizer wrote it; and, for each notebook, whether a repository of that name exists under the same owner, whether it is private, internal or public, and whether GitHub counts you its administrator, which GitHub gives in the same answer. On a public or internal repository it reads none of these, since a notebook names your files. When you propose a notebook, change one or take one out, it asks for catalog.json’s version once more and writes notebooks.json on that branch, as you, over the version it read, so that a change the organizer made meanwhile is never written over; when you take out the last notebook it deletes the file, and whatever else the organizer wrote in it goes with it. Where a notebook’s repository is public or internal and GitHub does not say you are not its administrator, the side panel offers Make private: once you confirm, after a question that says what GitHub erases with the change (its stars and watchers), what becomes of its forks and, for a public repository, what stops with it (on a free plan its GitHub Pages site and the enforcement of its rulesets and branch protection, its code scanning unless its owner has GitHub Code Security, and its secret scanning and push protection unless its owner has GitHub Secret Protection), the page asks GitHub, as you, to make that repository private, which takes SymphonyBoard’s Administration permission (or, with a pasted token, the token’s), and shows what GitHub answers; it changes nothing else about the repository. It writes nothing else: in your browser’s storage only the width of its side panel, kept with the layout (above), and nothing to the drive, of which Microsoft is asked nothing. The repository a notebook names is made by the notebook skill in a Claude session, not by the page. The file the tab writes stays on the private repository’s branch, where GitHub keeps it as it keeps any file, readable by whoever may read that repository, and Make private changes only the visibility GitHub keeps for a notebook’s repository; the developer receives none of either.

The aggregates the collector reads are as the section on field metrics says, whether or not you use the pages. The pages never show a repository’s Claude secret, which GitHub never gives back, and they take no Claude token. The Tokens page has no box to paste one into. Its “+ Add Token” has the repository’s workflow Token make the token on a runner instead, as the next paragraph says, so the most the page ever holds of it is the sealed box the run posts, which GitHub alone can open. Where the page makes the writes itself, it saves that box, as you, as the secret SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32, or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for the slot main. For an organization’s repository that is an organization secret, seen by the repository the page shows beside the repositories it reached already; for a personal account’s repository it is that repository’s own secret. It then writes, as you, for any slot but main, as an organization (or repository) variable, the list SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS, and in an organization adds the repository the page shows to the repositories that may read that list where it is shared with selected repositories, or shares a list it makes with that repository alone, as a tile’s save does (below); the slot’s label, if you gave one, is written with the slot’s settings, as below. The token goes nowhere else: not to the sign-in service, not to the developer, not into the browser’s storage, a log or the page.

“+ Add Token” on the same page makes the token where it is needed, through a run of the repository’s workflow Token, so no Claude token is ever pasted into the page. On your press, the page opens an issue on the repository, as you, and starts the repository’s workflow Token (the template’s .github/workflows/token.yml) with the issue’s number and, where the page makes the writes itself (below), the public key GitHub gives for your organization’s secrets (for a personal account’s repository, the repository’s), or, where the Token workflow makes them for you (below), the word pool and, where the run is on another of the organization’s repositories, the id of the repository the token is for. The run is on GitHub Actions, on the repository’s owner’s Actions allowance: it installs Claude Code, runs claude setup-token, and posts on the issue the claude.ai sign-in link that prints. Where the page makes the writes itself (below), the run holds no secret; where the Token workflow makes them for you (below), the run also holds SymphonyBoard’s private key, from which it mints the App’s installation token once before Claude Code is installed, to look for a token of yours in the pool and lend it where it finds one, and revokes that token before the sign-in starts, and, where it found none, once more after Claude Code has gone, to make the writes. The page shows that link as a button. You sign in to claude.ai as the account to add and press Authorize, and claude.ai shows a code; you paste it into the page, which posts it on the issue as a comment of yours. The run reads it, deletes that comment, and hands it to claude setup-token; the code is good only once and only to that run, which holds the other half of the sign-in. The run takes the Claude token out of what Claude Code prints before anything is written to its log and, where the page makes the writes itself, seals it there with the public key the page gave and posts only the sealed box on the issue, which GitHub alone can open. The page saves that box as the next free slot and, while CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN is not set, as that secret too, writes the list SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS as above, and closes the issue. On an organization’s repository, where you are an owner of the organization the page makes those writes as you; where you are a collaborator but not an owner, GitHub refuses you the write, so the Token workflow itself makes it on SymphonyBoard’s installation token (the section above): the same sealed slot, marked in the settings variable SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS as yours by your GitHub login and account id, the list SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS, and the repository on the lists of repositories that may read the three; where you have a token in the pool already, that one is lent to the repository instead, unless it is in the organization’s keeping (below), which such a lend lends nowhere more, and no sign-in is asked, the run recording your account id in that token’s settings where they named you by your login alone, as those of a token stored before the pool kept account ids do and those of a token an owner of the organization added or marked as yours on the Tokens page do, since the page writes a login and no account id; and nothing else. Where the repository the page shows is an organization’s and has no workflow Token of its own, as one adopted for the claim protocol alone before the adoption brought that workflow has none until it merges a pull request the Sync run offers it, where that run offers one (the section on the Sync run says where it offers none, as to a repository that opted out of it), or one where a file of its own kept that workflow out, the page reads, as you, the records of up to a hundred of the organization’s repositories you can see, the most recently pushed, and, one by one, whether each that is not archived, carries the topic symphony and takes your pushes has its workflow Token turned on, keeps the first such repository in the open page’s memory, and opens the issue and starts the run there instead, the issue’s text naming the repository the token is for. The token then goes to that repository and not to the one the run is on: through the page’s own writes where you are an owner, and otherwise through the run, which the page gives that repository’s id and which first reads, on SymphonyBoard’s token, that repository’s record, to see that it is the organization’s, and your permission on it, to see that you may write to it, and lends nothing where either is not so. Only a run started by hand, as the page starts it, is given another repository; a run an issue starts lends only to the repository the issue is on or, for a lend with no say (below), only to the repositories the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO names. The Claude token is never on the page, in the issue, in the run’s log, at the sign-in service or shown to the developer by GitHub, though on that path it is held in the developer’s own organization, with what that allows (the section above). The issue and its comments stay on the repository the page opened it on, as any issue does, and anyone who can read that repository can read them, everyone where it is public: the link, the sealed box or the slot’s number with, where your token was in the pool already, the ids of every repository it is lent to or, for a token in the organization’s keeping, the word organization in their place, until the run deletes it, the code, and, where the page opened the issue on another of the organization’s repositories, the name of the repository the token is for, which they read there even where that repository is private and they may not read it, none of which gives a Claude token to anyone else. Delete the issue on GitHub if you want it gone. Beside the button, the page links the Claude GitHub App’s install page on GitHub, opened for the one repository, unless the page can see that App installed on all of the organization’s repositories already; installing it is your own press on GitHub.

Where you are not an owner of the organization, the page also shows a box “Your token”, with “Where is my token lent?”, “Delete my token” and, beside each repository it lists, “Take back”. Each press opens an issue on the repository, as you, and starts the Token workflow’s manage job, which runs on SymphonyBoard’s installation token for the one token in the pool whose settings name you, by your GitHub login and your account’s id or, for a token whose settings name you by your login alone, as those of one stored before the pool kept account ids or of one an owner of the organization added or marked as yours on the Tokens page do, by that login, after which the run records your account id on it, and for no other: it posts on the issue the slot’s number and the ids of the repositories the slot’s secret reaches, never their names, since the issue’s readers may not be allowed to see them; or takes the secret off the one repository you named and, whether or not your token reached it, the two variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS with it where no other of the numbered slots SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32 reaches that repository, none of them being on in every repository or in every private one, whatever the slot main, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, reaches (the section above), and then posts on the issue, as a list does, the slot’s number and the ids of the repositories the secret still reaches, unless your token is in the organization’s keeping (below), which the run refuses to take off a repository, saying that you may still delete it; or deletes the slot’s secret first and then its settings and its place in SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS, leaving those of another token stored in the freed slot meanwhile, and, where the secret was on in selected repositories and none of the other numbered slots is on in every repository or in every private one, takes the two variables off each repository it was lent to that no other of the numbered slots reaches, whatever the slot main reaches (the section above). The page closes the issue when the run has answered, and shows a listed repository by name only where your own token can read it. Deleting the secret does not revoke the token, which you revoke on claude.ai; a deletion that stops partway, after the secret is gone but before its settings, leaves your mark on a slot with no token, which the next store into that slot writes over.

Both runs can also be started without the page, by an issue, since GitHub lets a workflow be started by hand only by someone who may write to the repository, while anyone who may open an issue there, on a public repository anyone with a GitHub account, may lend a token or manage their own. An issue whose first line is <!-- symphony-token: lend --> starts the sign-in run above for the issue’s author: the run posts the claude.ai sign-in link as a comment on the issue, takes the code only from a comment of the author’s, bare or under the page’s mark, deletes that comment, seals the token and stores it in a free slot of the organization’s pool as the author’s, marked by login and account id and lent to the repository the issue is on; where the author has a token in the pool already, that one is lent instead, unless it is in the organization’s keeping (below), and no sign-in is asked. An issue whose first line is <!-- symphony-token: manage --> and whose second line says list, revoke and a repository’s id, or delete does for the author’s own token what the box above does; a token whose settings name its owner by login alone, as those of one stored before the pool kept account ids or of one an owner of the organization added or marked on the Tokens page do, is refused from an issue, since a login can pass to someone else once an account is renamed or deleted, and the author is told to press Add Token on the page once. The run closes the issue when it is done, whether or not it succeeded, unless the run is cancelled or runs out of time; a code posted after the run has stopped stays until you delete it. Such an issue holds what the page’s issues hold: the link, the code until the run deletes it, and the run’s answers, the slot’s number, with the ids of the repositories it reaches when the run lends or lists it or takes it back from one, or a word that the run stopped and why, which may quote the last words Claude Code printed with any token and the code taken out; never the Claude token, and no repository’s name. In crowd mode the run reads the issue’s comments, so as to say it once, says on the issue only that the repository holds no Claude token, and closes it as not planned. Outside crowd mode, where the repository has no Actions variable SDLC_APP_ID, which names the App beside its key (the section on what each App asks for), a lend asks for no sign-in and a manage touches no token: the run reads the issue’s comments, so as to say it once, says on the issue, with the repository’s own GitHub token, why it stopped, and closes the issue as not planned. In the Token workflow as the template holds it since version 34 of this statement, it says that the repository does not hold the App’s settings and so stores no token into a pool, and that an owner of the organization adds one with Add Token. In a copy of the whole template made before then, which keeps the Token workflow it was made with, an issue starts such a run only where the copy was made since 03:38 UTC on 2026-10-19, when the template’s Token workflow came to start on an issue, and there the job the issue asks for starts in the environment token-store, as the section on what each App asks for says, stops at the App’s token, and the run says only that it stopped.

A lend whose second line says organization is a lend with no say: the token is stored the same way, its settings also marked with the word organization, and lent not to the issue’s repository but to the repositories the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO names, a list of repository ids the organization’s owners keep on the Tokens page under “Tokens lent with no say run on”, which the page writes as them, readable by no repository’s workflows, since the run reads it with the App’s token (a list an earlier page wrote readable by the private repositories’ workflows, or by every repository’s, is closed so when an owner next opens the Tokens tab, its value kept); or to none while that list is empty, for an owner to place from the slot’s tile. Such a lender is told the slot’s number when the token is stored and, when they list it or when a lend touches a token of theirs already in the pool, that it is in the organization’s keeping, and learns no repository’s name or id from the run. A lend with no say from someone who has a token in the pool already puts that token in the organization’s keeping: it stays where it was lent, goes also where SYMPHONY_LEND_TO says, and from then on the run names no repository to them. The owners see the slot on the Tokens page with the lender’s login, lend it to more repositories or take it off one, and delete it; the lender can delete it at any time and lends it to more repositories only with another lend with no say, to the repositories SYMPHONY_LEND_TO names, though the run names none to them; only the owners take it off a repository. Since anyone with a GitHub account may do this on a public repository, the pool fills with what is offered: an owner deletes a slot from its tile, and GitHub’s own limits bound the issues and the runs. A store that stops partway, after the slot is marked as the lender’s but before the secret is written, leaves that mark on a slot with no token, which the next store takes over.

The page shows each token set as a tile, and on your press a tile’s settings: a name, the model and thinking strength its runs take, a lesser model for when the model’s weekly limit runs out, whether it comes back by itself when its limit resets, and Pause. The page writes them, as you, to the organization (or repository) variable SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, which the repository’s workers read, and the name to the slot’s label variable, and, in an organization, adds the repository the page shows to the repositories that may read each variable it writes where that variable is shared with selected repositories, or shares a variable it makes with that repository alone, whether or not any token is lent there; neither holds a token, and anyone who can read the workflows of a repository that may read them can read them, the settings giving the login of every token’s owner and the account id of everyone whose token the Token run stored, or later lent or managed for them from the page where the settings named them by their login alone. A tile’s X, after you confirm, deletes the slot’s secret, its label, its settings and its place in SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS, as you, adding the repository the page shows, in the same way, to the repositories that may read each of SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS it rewrites rather than deletes, and taking no repository off them; deleting the secret does not revoke the token, which you revoke on claude.ai. A slot can also be removed on GitHub under the organization’s Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions. Each token’s settings also hold an id, eight random hexadecimal digits the page or the Token run makes, and the GitHub login of the person it belongs to; a token the Token run stores also holds that person’s account id (since a login can pass to someone else once an account is renamed or deleted), as does one whose settings named its owner by login alone once the Token run has lent or managed it for them from the page, and, for a token lent with no say, the word organization, which a save of the tile’s settings keeps, the account id while the token still belongs to the same login. So an organization’s tokens pool in one place while each stays its owner’s: to show who may change which token, the page asks GitHub for your role in the organization, and it offers a token’s settings, its X and its repositories only to the token’s owner and to an owner of the organization. A tile’s dialog lists the repositories the token’s secret is on, from GitHub, and a tick adds or removes one, as you. A worker’s run in Actions labels the issue it worked token:<id>, with the repository’s own token, so the panel can credit each token, and its owner, with the issues it closed; the label holds no token, name or e-mail address. What they start, a worker’s run or the Claude workflow’s answer to a mention, runs on the token the repository holds, as the repository’s own workflows do. To stop: press “Forget the token”, which drops the token and the refresh token from the browser and, for a token from “Sign in with GitHub”, by GitHub’s page or by a code, asks GitHub through the service to revoke the token, save one the browser refused to store, which the page held in its memory alone and which runs out within eight hours, as above; a personal access token is revoked on GitHub under Settings, Developer settings, Personal access tokens, and the App’s authorization, which covers every token and refresh token it issued you, under Settings, Applications, Authorized GitHub Apps.

The control panel’s Folders tab

The control panel’s Folders tab, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/#folders, shows your OneDrive as a file explorer, in which you can also make, rename, move, copy, delete, upload, download and share its files and folders, and makes a repository of yours track files and folders of the drive, which the repository’s own workflow, drive-sync.yml, then keeps in step with the drive. It is a tab of the control panel’s one page: it uses the panel’s sign-in, whichever way you signed in, and works on the repository the panel’s bar has chosen. It reads nothing until you open it, or until it opens itself on Microsoft’s return (below). Once open, it reads with your GitHub token, for the chosen repository, the file .github/symphony/drive.json, whether the repository’s secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH is set and when it was last updated (never the secret itself, which GitHub gives nobody back) and whether its workflows .github/workflows/drive-sync.yml and .github/workflows/drive-catalog.yml are there. When you press “Find the repository I just made”, it reads GitHub’s list of the ten repositories your token reaches that were made last and, for each one not on the bar’s list yet whose entry there shows neither the template nor the topic symphony, that repository’s own record, to add to the list those made from the Symphony template or carrying the topic symphony and choose the newest, which the control panel then reads as it reads any repository you choose. Its link “Create a repository from the template” opens GitHub’s own form in a new tab, where you name the repository and create it on GitHub; while the template is internal to the developer’s enterprise, only the enterprise’s members can use that form, and anyone else adopts a repository through the front door, as the section on the adoption says. The page sends nothing there. Where GitHub refuses the tab even to say whether the repository’s secret is set, the tab says so as it opens, before you connect a drive, and offers no Track.

The tab no longer reads the drive organizer’s catalog, catalog.json on the repository’s branch drive-catalog, as versions 26 to 35 of this statement said it did while no drive was connected: it shows only the drive you connect. The Notebooks tab still reads that file (the control panel, above).

When you press Track it reads the repository’s record (its default branch and whether it is public), the names of what its default branch holds at its top, to refuse a folder the repository already holds there, such as one its checks run, unless it is the folder the repository tracks already, and its public key for secrets. Where the repository is public, Track writes nothing until you tick the box beside it that says what you tick will be readable by anyone, a box the tab shows for a public repository and never ticks for you. It then writes, as you, in this order: the secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH, the drive’s refresh token sealed in your browser with that key the way GitHub’s own secrets page seals one, so that GitHub alone can open it; the file drive.json, which names the provider, the folder in the repository, the name, the id and the drive’s id of each item you ticked and the day you connected, committed over the one already there, whose version it reads first, on the default branch or, where that branch takes only pull requests, on the branch symphony/drive, which it makes from the default branch’s head, or sets back to that head where a branch of that name is there already, so that it holds this one commit and nothing else, with a pull request for you to merge, or the one already open from that branch; and, only where the file went to the default branch, one run of drive-sync.yml started by hand. Where the file went to the default branch it also sets the repository’s Actions variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE to on, which says nothing of the drive and which whoever can read the repository’s settings can see, so that the workflow’s half-hourly schedule runs there; until it is set, the schedule starts nothing, and where the file waits in a pull request the variable waits for a later Track. Where your token may not save the secret, the page says so and writes nothing else; where the file cannot be written, the secret stays saved, and the page says so and starts no run; where the run cannot be started, the page says so and links the workflow’s page on GitHub, where you press “Run workflow”.

In a repository of an organization, Track saves the refresh token not in the repository but once for the organization, as the organization’s secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH, where all of these hold: the repository has no secret of that name of its own, which would take the organization’s place there; the repository is public, or the organization’s plan is a paid one, since GitHub lets a private repository on GitHub Free read no organization secret; your token may read the organization’s public key for secrets, as an owner’s may; the secret’s list of repositories can be read whole; and the organization holds no such secret yet, or its variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID names the same drive you connected, so that one person’s Track does not replace another person’s drive, save where two Tracks with different drives run at the same moment, which the page then says. To tell, it reads the organization’s record, of which it uses only its plan’s name, that key, whether that secret is there, the variable’s value, a drive’s id, which says nothing of what the drive holds, and the list of repositories the secret is shared with, page by page. It then saves the token sealed in your browser as that secret, shared with selected repositories only, those already on its list and this one, never with all of the organization’s repositories or its private ones, and saves the drive’s id as the organization’s variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID, shared with the same repositories, which whoever can read the organization’s or those repositories’ settings can see, and reads the variable back, to say on the page when another Track wrote it in the meantime. Otherwise, or where GitHub refuses the organization’s secret, Track saves the repository’s own secret as above; a repository that once took the organization’s secret stays on its list until an owner of the organization takes it off there. So one connection serves every repository of the organization that tracks the same drive, and a new connection, pressed in any of them, replaces the token for all of them. A repository that carries the workflow .github/workflows/drive-catalog.yml and not drive-sync.yml, the drive catalog’s own repository, takes from Track the secret alone: Track writes no drive.json there and starts no run. “Sync now”, which the tab shows once the repository tracks a drive, reads the default branch and starts one run of drive-sync.yml on it.

When the Folders tab opens a repository that tracks a drive already, which it tells by the workflow drive-sync.yml there, the file drive.json on its default branch, the repository’s own secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH set and the connection that drive.json records not run out, it also reads the repository’s Actions variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE and, where that is not on, sets it to on, as you, without a press of Track, the owner’s choice of 2026-10-20, so that a drive tracked before Track set the switch syncs each half hour. It writes nothing else, reads no drive and starts no run, and says on the page when it set the variable or could not.

The drive’s side goes through Microsoft and the sign-in service. When you first open the tab, it asks the sign-in service which drives it is set up for, and the service answers with the public client id of the developer’s Microsoft app registration, or that OneDrive is not set up yet. When you press “Connect OneDrive”, the page keeps in the tab’s own storage a one-time value, a one-time secret it made for this connection, the panel’s query (the repository it showed) and the GitHub login the panel names, and sends your browser to Microsoft, which asks you on its own page whether Symphony may read and write your files (Files.ReadWrite) and keep that access when you are away (offline_access); for a work or school account, the organization’s settings may require its administrator’s approval first. Microsoft sends your browser back with a one-time code to the control panel’s own address, https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/control/, the page GitHub’s sign-in returns to as well; the page tells the two apart by which of the one-time values it kept the returned one matches, takes the code out of the address before anything else, forgets what it kept, and the other one-time values where a sign-in or a connection was left pending beside it, puts the panel’s query back as it was and, whatever came of the return, opens the Folders tab. A code that comes back with any other value is never sent for a drive’s tokens. The page sends the code, with the one-time secret, to the sign-in service, which adds the client secret of the developer’s Microsoft app registration, asks Microsoft for the drive’s access token and refresh token, and hands both back. Leaving the page for Microsoft ends the renewals of a GitHub sign-in made for one tab alone, as leaving it for any other page does (the control panel, above), and that sign-in’s token serves out its eight hours.

The page keeps the drive’s two tokens in its memory alone, never in the browser’s storage, the address or a log, and only for the GitHub account the panel named when you pressed “Connect OneDrive” (or, pressed while it named nobody, the first it names on the return): reloading or leaving the page, any sign-out, pressing “Forget the token” among them, or a sign-in as another GitHub account forgets them, and you press “Connect OneDrive” again; Track drops them once the secret and the file are written. With the access token the page reads, from your browser and as you, through Microsoft Graph, the drive’s type and its owner’s display name, to say which drive is connected, and its id, to refuse at Track an item the repository tracked from another drive, and the names, kinds, sizes, dates, ids, paths in the drive and web addresses of the files and folders in the folders you open, to draw the list you tick in, laid out as a file explorer with a tree of the folders you open in it, each read asking Microsoft also for a small picture of each file, which your browser then loads from Microsoft’s own servers with no token and no referrer (where Microsoft refuses it as a bad request, the page reads the list again without the pictures and asks for none again until the page is reloaded; a search asks for none); nothing of that list leaves your browser but the name, the id and the drive’s id of what you tick, which go into drive.json. When you open a file from the list, by a double click, Enter or its menu, the page hands your browser the file’s address and nothing else: a Word, Excel, PowerPoint or Visio file goes to that program on your computer through Office’s own address scheme (ms-word: and the like), at the file’s address on your drive (for a personal OneDrive, d.docs.live.net, your drive’s id and the file’s path; for a work or school drive, the address OneDrive gave), so that the program opens it from the drive, signs in to Microsoft itself and saves your edits there; any other file, or one you choose to open in the browser, opens on OneDrive’s own page in a new tab. Your browser may ask first whether to open the program. Nothing is sent to the developer, the sign-in service or GitHub when you open a file. When the access token runs out during a sitting, the page sends the refresh token to the service, which answers with a new access token.

The explorer’s own actions also go from your browser to Microsoft Graph alone, as you and with the same access token, each only when you press it, and each changes your drive as the same action in OneDrive would. New folder makes a folder named New folder, numbered where that name is taken, in the folder you are in, and then lets you rename it. Rename gives an item the name you type, and where the item is one you ticked, that name is the one Track writes into drive.json. Delete asks you on the page first and then deletes each item you chose, one request each, into your drive’s recycle bin, from which OneDrive lets you restore it, and unticks an item you had ticked. Upload, by its button or by dropping files on the list, sends each file you chose from your computer into the folder you are in: a file of up to 4 MB in one request, a larger one through an upload session Microsoft opens, in pieces of about 3.3 MB sent to the address Microsoft gives for it with no token; where a file of that name is there, the page asks you first whether to replace it, keep both or skip it. Download asks Microsoft for a short-lived address of the file and hands it to your browser, which saves the file from Microsoft with no token; the page never reads the file’s contents. Cut, copy and paste, or dragging items onto a folder, move or copy the items you chose into the folder you paste in (to know the drive’s top folder the page reads its id once for each connection); Microsoft makes a copy in its own time, so the page reads the folder again a few seconds later to show it; a copy whose name is taken gets a numbered name, and a move whose name is taken is refused and the page says so. Share makes, only when you press Create link, a sharing link to one item, for viewing or for editing, as you choose: on a work or school drive one that works for people in your organization, its default, or for anyone who has the link; on a personal drive (or on any drive whose type the page could not read) one for anyone who has the link, the only kind it offers; whoever you then give the link to can open the item, and edit it where you chose editing, until you remove the link in OneDrive, which the page does not do. Copy puts the link on your device’s clipboard. Properties reads one item’s name, id, size, kind and file details, folder and the number of items it holds, dates, web address and whether it is shared, and who made it and last changed it (Microsoft’s record of each, of which the page shows the display name); for several items it adds up what the list already shows. The preview pane, off until you turn it on, shows the one file you choose: for an image, a larger picture read from Microsoft; for any other file, Microsoft’s own preview, from a short-lived address Microsoft makes for it, drawn in a frame limited by the browser’s sandbox on Microsoft’s own site with no referrer, or, where Microsoft makes none, a larger picture; a folder reads nothing. Search, when you press Enter, sends the words you typed to Microsoft to find the matching files and folders anywhere in the drive, up to two thousand of them; typing without pressing Enter only filters the list already shown, in your browser. The views, the sort order and choosing several items with Shift or Ctrl ask nothing of anyone. The page keeps the view, the sort order, whether the preview is on, what you have chosen, what you cut or copied, the words you searched for and the preview’s addresses in the open page’s memory alone, with nothing of them in the browser’s storage, the address or a log, unless you press “Ask in claude.ai”, which carries the words of a search shown, as the bar’s section says, and forgets them, with the drive’s tokens, when you reload or leave the page. None of these actions sends anything to GitHub, the sign-in service or the developer.

The repository’s workflow does the same at the start of every sync: on GitHub’s runners it sends the secret, your refresh token, to the service, or to the address the repository’s variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_TOKEN_URL names instead, and with the access token it gets back it reads at Microsoft the items the default branch’s drive.json names and what a ticked folder holds, six levels down (until a pull request carrying a new list merges, the newly saved secret is used with the list already there), brings what changed in the drive into the repository by pull request, sends up what changed in the repository and, where a file changed on both sides, puts the repository’s copy beside the drive’s in the same folder; it touches nothing else in the drive. The drive organizer’s workflow, drive-organize.yml, where a private repository runs it, and the drive catalog’s workflow, drive-catalog.yml, which has no step organize and always starts from the drive’s top, each trade the same secret at the same route for an access token in the same way and read at Microsoft Graph alone, the workflow itself using no other connector, the names, kinds, sizes, dates, ids, folders and web addresses of the files and folders under what drive.json names for it (the whole drive where that is its top), up to 20,000 entries, and the contents of a sample of them, at most 400 files of up to 5 MB each and 120 MB in all; where it starts from the drive’s top, the folders Microsoft 365 keeps there (Apps, Attachments, Meetings, Recordings, Notebooks, Desktop, Documents, Pictures and the Teams and Copilot chat folders) it lists by name without reading inside. Each writes what it found, the list and, for each file of the sample, a text of at most 1,500 characters taken from it (a document’s headings, opening and comments, a sheet’s header, first rows and column totals, a deck’s slide text), to the branch drive-catalog of that repository as one commit on top of what the branch holds, where whoever can read the repository can read it, and changes nothing in the drive. The organizer’s step organize, when started, also gives that list and those texts to Claude, on the repository’s own Claude token and under Anthropic’s terms for that account, and opens issues in the repository naming the files, folders and links of the projects Claude proposes. What comes down, and drive.json with the names of what you ticked, can be read by whoever can read the repository, and by anyone where it is public, and the new review comments in its Word documents become tasks, issues of the repository, readable the same way. The route of the service that trades a refresh token for an access token answers whoever sends it one, the workflow’s request, which comes from no page, among them. The access Microsoft grants reaches every file of your OneDrive, not only what you ticked, so whoever can run a workflow on the repository, anyone who may write to it, can read the secret and, through that route, reach the whole drive until the token lapses or you withdraw the access; where the secret is the organization’s, that is anyone who may write to any repository on its list, which an owner of the organization sees and changes under the organization’s Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions; deleting the secret withdraws nothing at Microsoft. You withdraw it at https://account.live.com/consent/Manage for a personal account, or in My Apps, https://myapps.microsoft.com, for a work or school account, where its administrator may have to. The service’s word on which drives it is set up for, a public client id, is given to whoever asks; every other route answers the site’s pages alone, as the control panel section says. The service keeps nothing of any of it: no store, no cookie and no log of its own of the code, the tokens or you, and its host’s request logs are off, as that section says; the refresh token passes through it on Connect and on every sync and rests only in your repository’s secret, and the newer refresh token Microsoft issues with each access token is dropped there. A Microsoft refresh token lasts 90 days, and the workflow cannot keep the newer one (where the secret is the organization’s, one day for every repository it serves), so the tab shows the day you connected, which drive.json records, and the day by which to press “Connect OneDrive” again and then Track, which replaces the secret and that day, and once that day has passed it says that the connection has run out and that every sync since stops before it reaches the drive. Google Drive is not offered: Google’s own picker takes a browser API key, which the developer has declined, so the page connects no other drive and the service refuses any provider but OneDrive. The developer receives nothing from the tab, the service, the workflow or the organizer’s workflow; what Claude receives is under your Claude account’s terms.

The App’s server, where it is run

SymphonyBoard’s webhook server, when the developer turns the webhook on, receives from GitHub each event the App subscribes to, acts on pull request events only (opened, synchronize, reopened, ready for review, converted to draft, edited) and logs and ignores the rest. For a pull request event it reads the action, the installation’s id, the repository’s full name and the pull request’s number from the delivery, then reads the pull request from the API (its head and base, its body, whether it is a draft and its head commit) and whether the claim file for its issue exists at that commit, and writes one thing: the check run sdlc/protocol on that commit, with a title and a summary that lists each protocol problem in one line. It posts no comment. It verifies every delivery’s signature before reading it, keeps installation tokens in memory for at most an hour and stores nothing on disk; its log holds one line per delivery with the time, the delivery’s id, the event, the action, the repository’s full name, the duration and a short outcome, and never a token, a payload or a person’s words.

Keys and tokens

Each App’s private key is the developer’s and is never given to anyone: it lives in the Actions secrets of the developer’s own repositories and in the server’s environment, outside any repository; the Sync run signs the App’s credential with SymphonyBoard’s key itself, with openssl, which it hands the key through a pipe and never in a file. Every token minted from it is an installation token that lives one hour, asked with the fewest permissions the step needs (metadata alone to resolve a number, contents read to read, the four write permissions only for the adoption itself, Contents, Pull requests and Workflows (write) and Metadata (read) for the Sync run, one installation at a time, Symphony Setup’s Secrets and Variables only for lending the requester’s own tokens) and revoked as soon as the step is done where the code can, except in the Token workflow of the developer’s own organization, which mints it with every permission the installation has, for all the organization’s repositories the App reaches, in a job that runs only the default branch’s script and that anyone who may open an issue there can start; the token for the look at the pool is revoked before Claude Code starts, the others when the job ends. The client secrets the sign-in service holds, SymphonyBoard’s and the developer’s Microsoft app registration’s, live in that service’s settings on Cloudflare, outside any repository, and go from there only to GitHub’s and Microsoft’s endpoints that issue tokens and, for SymphonyBoard’s, to GitHub’s that revokes one; the two device routes of sign-in by code send no client secret, asking GitHub with the client id alone. No token, key or signature is ever printed to a log.

What the Apps never do

They send nothing to any service but GitHub’s own API. They have no analytics, no error reporting and no third party. SymphonyBoard holds Administration only for the control panel’s Share tab, which reads the invitations waiting and, when you ask, invites a collaborator, changes a collaborator’s or an invitation’s role, removes a collaborator or withdraws an invitation, and for its Notebooks tab’s Make private, which makes a notebook’s repository private when you press it and confirm, each as you, and uses it for nothing else; Symphony Setup holds it where you installed it, uses it only during an adoption run, and stays installed until you uninstall it. They read your repository’s code only as the adoption and the Sync run above say (the tree listing, in the adoption a one-commit checkout of the default branch, in the Sync run the lines of changed files that GitHub’s comparison of your default branch with the branch symphony/sync shows, and the few files named), never to keep or send it. Apart from what the control panel writes as you, with SymphonyBoard’s token, when you press the button that says so, as the section on the control panel says, of which a repository made private on the Notebooks tab is not wholly yours to undo, since GitHub erases its stars and watchers with the change and leaves a public repository’s forks public and detached from it, or makes an internal repository’s forks private and removes those of people without access to it, none of which making it public again brings back, they never write to a repository but the adoption’s branch, pull request, labels, issue and settings and the Sync run’s branch symphony/sync and pull request, each of them yours to undo, the git objects in which the Sync run writes the files, the tree and the commit it offers, and the README that begins a repository with no commit, and, in an organization whose Symphony Setup installation has Secrets and Variables, the lists of repositories that read the requester’s own token slots and the pool’s two variables, as the section on what each App asks for says; in the pool of Claude tokens of the developer’s own organization, the only one holding SymphonyBoard’s key, the Token workflow writes with SymphonyBoard’s token only what the section on the control panel says, a slot, the two variables and the lists of repositories that read them, for the person who lends or manages the token. They never read a Claude credential (the control panel’s pages never see one, only, where a page saves the token itself, the sealed box the Token workflow posts, which GitHub alone can open; a token the Token workflow makes is plain only on the runner until it is sealed, beside SymphonyBoard’s token where the run stores it for a lender, as the section on organization permissions says), and nothing here runs on anyone’s Claude account but the one a project’s own maintainer chooses to run the judge with. The control panel’s Folders tab and the sign-in service, neither of them an App, talk to Microsoft for the OneDrive you connect, as the section on the Folders tab says; the Apps themselves send Microsoft nothing. Nor is the control panel an App: its pages link the site’s typefaces from Google Fonts, which your browser asks Google for as they load, as the section on the control panel says, and the Apps themselves send Google nothing.

Uninstalling

Uninstalling SymphonyBoard stops the collector from reading anything of yours and the Sync run from reading anything of yours or offering you anything, as taking a repository off the installation’s list does for that repository, and undoes nothing in your repository: the files, labels, branch, settings and issues the adoption made, and the branch symphony/sync and the pull request of an offer, stay yours. Symphony Setup stays installed after the run, acting only during an adoption run; uninstalling it, at any time, from the repository’s or the organization’s Settings, GitHub Apps, also undoes nothing in your repository.

Children

Symphony is for people who administer GitHub repositories. It is not directed at children.

Changes

A new version of this statement is published at https://openspineconsortium.com/symphony/apps-privacy.html and in the front door repository, github.com/OpenSpineConsortium/symphony-start, whose PRIVACY.md is this text.

Version 40 says that the Folders tab, when it opens a repository that tracks a drive already, its workflow drive-sync.yml, its drive.json on the default branch and its own secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH there and the connection not run out, reads the repository’s variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE and, where that is not on, sets it to on, as you, without a press of Track, so that a drive tracked before Track set the switch syncs each half hour; it writes nothing else and says on the page that it did. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.

Version 39 says that the Folders tab’s Track takes the organization’s secret only where the repository is public or the organization’s plan is a paid one, for which it reads the organization’s record and uses only its plan’s name, and only where the secret’s list of repositories reads whole, which it reads page by page; that where GitHub refuses the organization’s secret it saves the repository’s own; that it reads SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID back after writing it; that a repository that once took the organization’s secret stays on its list; and that it sets SYMPHONY_DRIVE only where drive.json went to the default branch. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.

Version 38 says that in an organization’s repository the Folders tab’s Track saves a drive’s refresh token once for the organization, as its secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH, and the drive’s id as its variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID, each shared with selected repositories alone, adding each repository that tracks the drive to their lists, with SymphonyBoard’s organization permissions Secrets and Variables it already held for the Tokens page, where the repository has no secret of its own, the organization’s public key is yours to read and the organization holds no such secret or one for the same drive, and otherwise the repository’s own secret as before, so another person’s drive never replaces it; that anyone who may write to any repository on the list can then reach the whole drive; and that a new connection replaces the token, and its 90-day lapse, for every repository the secret serves. It says that in a repository carrying the drive catalog’s workflow, drive-catalog.yml, and no drive sync, Track saves the secret alone, writing no drive.json and starting no run, and that workflow walks the drive from its top as the organizer’s does, with no step organize. It says that Track also sets the repository’s Actions variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE, with SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Variables it already held for the Tokens page, so that the drive sync’s schedule runs only where a drive is tracked, and that the Sync run adds the drive sync’s workflow and its scripts where an adopted repository lacks them, as it adds the Token workflow. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.

Version 37 adds the environment token-store to what Symphony Setup makes in an adoption run, of either kind, as the section on the adoption says: it reads the repository’s default branch from the record it already reads, asks GitHub whether the repository has an environment of that name, through the environment’s list of deployment protection apps, which Administration reads, and where it has none makes one whose deployment branches are the default branch alone, with the Administration on the repository the Setup App already holds. It reads and writes nothing else; the environment holds no secret and no variable; the pull request says whether it was made, was there already or was not set up, quoting GitHub where it refused; and the run’s public log says only that, per setting. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.

Version 36 adds the Folders tab’s own actions on your OneDrive, as the section on the Folders tab says: new folder, rename, delete into the recycle bin, upload, download, cut, copy and paste, sharing links for viewing or editing, properties, a preview pane, a search of the whole drive and small pictures of the files in the list, each sent from your browser to Microsoft Graph alone, as you, with the access Microsoft already granted for the drive (Files.ReadWrite), and each only when you press it; what the explorer keeps it keeps in the open page’s memory alone. It says that the tab no longer reads the drive organizer’s catalog, which version 26 added, and that the drive organizer’s workflow reads the drive through Microsoft Graph alone with the repository’s drive secret and the sign-in service’s route, as drive-sync.yml does, lists without reading inside the folders Microsoft 365 keeps at the drive’s top, writes the list and texts of up to 1,500 characters from a sample of the files to the branch drive-catalog of a private repository, and, in its step organize, gives them to Claude on the repository’s own Claude token and opens issues for the projects Claude proposes. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.

Version 35 adds sign-in by code, GitHub’s device flow, built for the control panel installed as an app and switched off until the developer turns it on, as the section on the control panel says: while it is off no page offers a code; once it is on, a press of the installed app’s “Sign in with GitHub”, or in a browser’s tab of “Sign in with a code instead”, has the sign-in service’s route /device ask GitHub for a code with SymphonyBoard’s client id alone and no client secret, and the page holds the device code in the open page’s memory alone and sends it to the service’s route /device/token, at most once every five seconds, which passes it to GitHub with the client id and no client secret until you have typed the short code at https://github.com/login/device and allowed SymphonyBoard; the page then keeps what the sign-in by GitHub’s page keeps, save where the browser refuses to store the token, which a sign-in by code, needing no storage to finish, can meet: there the page holds it in its memory alone, never renews it, and “Forget the token”, or a sign-in by code or a pasted token that takes its place, drops it without asking GitHub to revoke it, so it stays good until it runs out within eight hours; and the service keeps nothing of it. It says that “Enable Device Flow”, which sign-in by code needs ticked on SymphonyBoard, lets anyone ask GitHub for a SymphonyBoard code and talk a person into typing it, which hands whoever asked a token that acts as that person, so the page warns beside every code to type only one started on that page a moment ago; and that such a sign-in’s refresh token renews at GitHub with the client id alone, each renewal good for six months more, so that it lasts until it is revoked or goes six months unrenewed, and where you revoke it; and that “Forget the token” asks GitHub to revoke each sign-in’s token that the tab’s own storage or the browser’s storage holds, and no other, so not one the browser refused to store, while whether GitHub then refuses such a sign-in’s refresh token too is not established. It names, as no earlier version did, the stylesheet of Google Fonts that the control panel and the cost page link for the site’s typefaces, Newsreader, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono, as the site’s other Symphony pages do, which your browser asks Google for, with the font files it names, as the pages load, with nothing of the page’s own in those requests, the stylesheet’s naming the page it came from by the site’s address alone and each font file’s naming the site by its origin and the stylesheet by Google’s own address alone, as browsers do unless set otherwise. And it says that the control panel installs as an app, the same page in a window of its own, whose “Sign in with GitHub” may come back from GitHub’s page to your browser rather than to the app, where the page sends the code nowhere and the code signs nobody in, while the app keeps what the press kept, as a tab does, until another press, a return or the clearing of that storage ends it, and that where the app shares its browser’s storage with that browser’s tabs it reads a sign-in or a token kept there with “Keep me signed in” ticked, and its “Forget the token” forgets that for those tabs too; earlier versions said that GitHub sends your browser back to the page, which holds in a browser’s tab alone. It also says, as no earlier version did, what a press of “Sign in with GitHub” keeps in the tab’s own storage until GitHub’s return reaches the page, or for as long as the sign-in is left unfinished: a one-time value, the sign-in’s one-time secret, whether “Keep me signed in” is ticked and the page’s query, the repository it showed. It corrects the section on the control panel’s Dependencies tab, which said that the tab writes nothing to your browser’s storage, as was so until its row of tiles came: where a repository has two charts or more, the page keeps there which of them you last chose, by the repository’s name and the chart’s, until you choose another, and neither “Forget the token” nor taking the repository off your list removes it; the list of what the page keeps in your browser now names it too. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 34 adds the Sync run, symphony-template#257, as the section of that name says: a workflow of the developer’s in the template’s own repository that, whenever the board’s, tidy, metrics or Token workflow, scripts/tokens.py or any file under tools/ changes there, once a week and by hand, walks every installation of SymphonyBoard on the App’s own key and, in each repository an installation reaches but the template’s and the front door’s own, a fork and one archived or disabled, reads the default branch’s newest commit and the listing of its tree, and, where that branch holds docs/agents/PROTOCOL.md, the text of the switches .github/symphony-sync, .github/symphony-adopt and .github/sdlc-adopt, and, where the repository has not opted out with off in one of them, holds no .github/workflows/protocol.yml, which every copy of the whole template holds unless its owner has removed it and none adopted for the protocol alone does, so that a copy of the whole template, the front door’s or one made with “Use this template”, is passed over with nothing written while it keeps that workflow, and a file needs changing, the twenty newest pull requests from the branch symphony/sync and, unless none of the App’s among them is open and the newest of the App’s was closed unmerged offering the same files, GitHub’s comparison of the default branch with that branch, where it exists, with lines of the files changed on it, and, where every commit the branch holds beyond the default branch is the App’s own or a merge and an open pull request of the App’s offers the same files, the record of the branch’s newest commit; it writes nothing where none of the App’s pull requests among them is open and the newest of the App’s was closed unmerged offering the same files, where a commit the branch holds beyond the default branch is neither the App’s own nor a merge or the branch holds more commits beyond the default branch than GitHub’s comparison lists, or where an open pull request of the App’s offers the same files and its branch already holds one commit straight on the default branch’s newest commit; otherwise it writes the files it offers, a tree and a commit on the default branch’s newest commit as git objects in the repository, the branch symphony/sync, which it makes or moves by force, and one pull request, or a new description for the one open, writing the offer and moving the branch again on each later run that gets that far while GitHub refuses to open that pull request, as it does while one someone else opened from the branch stands open, offering the newer versions of the vendored library and of the board’s, tidy, metrics and Token workflows with their scripts, replacing only files that hold a version the template once held, adding only the Token workflow with its scripts and, to a unit the repository has by its workflow or, for the library, by tools/VENDORED, every file of that unit the repository lacks, and never offering again a pull request closed unmerged while the files it would bring, each path with the template’s version of it, are the same; it does so on an installation token with Contents, Pull requests and Workflows (write) and Metadata (read), revoked after each installation’s repositories whatever GitHub answers, and its log, which whoever may read the template reads, counts outcomes and names no repository. SymphonyBoard asks for no new permission for it: the list of what SymphonyBoard asks for now names the Sync run under Contents, Pull requests and Workflows, and the sections on keys and tokens, on what the Apps never do and on uninstalling name it too. The introduction and the section on the adoption say that only a repository that holds the claim protocol without the whole template is offered newer files, and the section on the Sync run says that a copy of the whole template made since the template holds that run carries .github/workflows/sync.yml, whose runs there skip its one job. The section on the Sync run also says, as earlier versions did not, that a branch and a pull request an App makes, the adoption’s as well as the Sync run’s, start the workflows the repository runs on a push, a new branch or a pull request, in the versions the branch holds, save one that runs on pull_request_target, which runs in the default branch’s version. From symphony-start#76, the section on the adoption says that the protocol alone brings, beside the board’s, tidy and metrics workflows, the Token workflow with the scripts it runs, tools/token_run.py and the modules of the template it imports, today tools/sealbox.py, scripts/tokens.py and tools/pool.py, held back, as that section now says in full for each workflow it brings with a script, where something of the repository’s own, a file, a link or a folder, stands where one of them goes and is not a file, or a link to a file in the repository outside its .git, that holds the template’s version byte for byte, where a file of the repository’s own, or a link of its own to anything but a folder in the repository outside its .git, stands where one of their folders goes, where the repository ignores one of them, where Python would import a file of the repository’s own in place of one of them, or where one of them stays out with another workflow that imports it too, the board’s and the metrics workflows being held back also where the vendored library will not be the template’s, and that every issue opened starts it, its jobs skipping unless the issue asks it to lend or manage a token; so the section on the control panel no longer says that a repository adopted for the claim protocol alone has no workflow Token of its own, and says that one adopted for it before the adoption brought that workflow has none until it merges a pull request the Sync run offers it, where that run offers one, and that one where a file of its own kept that workflow out has none either. And from symphony-template#257 the section on what each App asks for, and the control panel’s passage on the runs an issue starts, say that where a repository has no variable SDLC_APP_ID, which names the App beside its key, the Token workflow’s two jobs that store a token into the pool and manage one there do not run, in the Token workflow as the template holds it from this version on, and a run asked for either outside crowd mode only says so on the issue, with the repository’s own token, and closes an issue that started it, where until then those jobs started there, GitHub recording each such run as a deployment to their environment token-store, which it made in the repository the first time one ran where the repository’s plan let it have environments, and stopped at the App’s token, in a copy made before 02:26 UTC on 2026-10-19 only after the Claude sign-in, the token then held on the runner and deleted unsaved, as they still do in a copy of the whole template made before then, which keeps the Token workflow it was made with, as the section on what each App asks for now says. That passage on the runs an issue starts also says, as version 33 did not, that a run in crowd mode reads the issue’s comments, so as to say it once, and closes the issue as not planned. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 33 adds the Notebooks tab’s Make private, the owner’s choice of 2026-10-19: where a notebook’s repository is public or internal, a button in its side panel makes it private on GitHub, as you, once you confirm, which SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Administration allows, as it allows the Share tab’s changes; the tab also reads, from the answer it already asked for, whether GitHub counts you the repository’s administrator, and offers the button only where GitHub does not say you are not. So the section on what the Apps never do no longer says that SymphonyBoard changes no setting with Administration, and the list of what SymphonyBoard asks for no longer says that it holds Administration for one thing only: Make private changes a repository’s visibility, when you press it and confirm. That section now also sets what the control panel writes as you, with SymphonyBoard’s token, apart from the writes it says the Apps never make, and says that a repository made private is not wholly yours to undo, since GitHub erases its stars and watchers and changes or removes its forks, none of which making it public again brings back. The list of what SymphonyBoard asks for, and the section on what the Apps never do, now name in full what the Share tab does with Administration (it reads the invitations waiting, invites, changes a role, removes a collaborator and withdraws an invitation), where earlier versions named only the invitation, and the section on the control panel names, as no earlier version did, the request to join that the Share tab and the Tokens page’s Add dialog open as an issue, as you, titled with your login and naming the repository, which anyone who can read the repository can read, which the Share tab lists from the repository’s open issues, and which an administrator answers there with Invite, or anyone the Share tab shows the repository’s collaborators to with a decline, each a comment on the issue and its close; the Share tab otherwise does what it did. It corrects version 32, which said that an adoption lends the person who asked a token they lent with no say: as symphony-start#72 was merged, the adoption never lends a token in the organization’s keeping, which only the organization’s owners place, counts it as none of the person’s and names it nowhere, so that where the person has no other token the run may lend, the pull request says that no token in the pool names them as its owner and the log says that no tokens were lent. The Version 32 entry below now names symphony-template#254, not #253, as the pull request that brought the Token workflow its rule for a token in the organization’s keeping, and this version says so too where it describes the Token workflow’s lends and take-backs: a lend that is not one with no say lends such a token nowhere more, and a take-back of it is refused. From symphony-template#253, it says that the Token workflow’s take-back and deletion take the two variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS off a repository no other of the numbered slots SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32 reaches, none of them being on in every repository or in every private one, whatever the slot main, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, reaches, a take-back whether or not the token reached that repository and a deletion only where the token was on in selected repositories, reading for that which repositories each of those other slots reaches, where earlier versions said the workflow never took a repository off them; that a deletion removes the secret first and its settings after, so that one stopped partway leaves a mark on an empty slot and no longer a token marked as no one’s; and that a deletion leaves the settings and the place in SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS of another token stored in the freed slot meanwhile. Until symphony-template#253 a deletion, or the recording of an account id on a slot stored before the pool kept them, also put the repository the run was on onto the lists of repositories that may read the variables it changed, which earlier versions did not say; the workflow no longer does, so what the text says the workflow adds to those lists, the repositories a token is lent to, needed no change for it. From symphony-template#249, it says that where the repository the control panel shows has no workflow Token of its own, the page reads the organization’s repositories to find one that has it, opens the issue and starts the run there, the issue’s text naming the repository the token is for, which anyone who can read the repository the issue is on can read, even where the repository the token is for is private, and lends the token to the repository it shows, or has the run lend it there once the run has read that repository’s record and the person’s permission on it. From symphony-template#251, it says that the template’s Claude workflow starts its job for a mention of @claude only by the repository’s owner, a member of its organization or a collaborator, so for anyone else’s mention GitHub marks the job skipped and no step runs. It also corrects what earlier versions said of the Tokens page and the Token workflow. The page has no box “Add or renew a slot” to paste a Claude token into, as earlier versions said, and seals nothing in your browser: its “+ Add Token”, which earlier versions called “Add a Claude account”, has the Token workflow make the token, the page holds at most the sealed box the run posts, the slots run to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32, and a secret the page saves is seen by the repository it shows, not by repositories you tick; the Actions permission names the page’s buttons by the names they have, “Read use now” and “Add Token”, and the box “Your token”; and a run that makes the writes for you holds SymphonyBoard’s private key, where earlier versions said the run holds no secret. The Token workflow’s reads are now named in full: the names and records of all the organization’s Actions secrets, the public key GitHub gives for sealing them, the records of SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS with their values, the second with the login of each slot’s owner and, where it holds one, their account id, and the GitHub record of the person it acts for, and SYMPHONY_LEND_TO only for a lend with no say; a lend from the page of a token already in the pool records its lender’s account id where its settings named them by login alone; and the issue of a token in the organization’s keeping carries the word organization in place of the repositories’ ids. The records on the branch pool the page reads also hold each single model’s weekly limit and whether Claude’s answer allowed the request. And a tile’s save and its X, in an organization, add the repository the page shows to the repositories that may read the variables they write, so the login of every token’s owner, and their account id where the settings hold one, reach that repository too, which earlier versions did not say. The section on the control panel now names the Tokens page’s own reads, as you, which earlier versions did not: the names and records of the Actions secrets where the tokens live, the name and value of every Actions variable there, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, SYMPHONY_LEND_TO for an owner of the organization, and CLAUDE_CROWD when you press Add Token. It says that the page gives the Token workflow the public key, and the run seals the token with it and posts the sealed box, only where the page makes the writes itself, and that where the run makes them the page gives it the word pool and, for a run on another repository, the id of the repository the token is for, where earlier versions said the page always gave the key. It says that a token’s settings name its owner by login alone not only where the token was stored before the pool kept account ids but also where an owner of the organization added it or marked it as someone’s on the Tokens page, which writes a login and no account id, so that such a token too is refused from an issue and, when the person presses for it on the page, given their account id, where earlier versions named only the older tokens. And it says that a take-back posts on the issue, as a list does, the slot’s number and the ids of the repositories the token still reaches, which earlier versions did not say. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 32 adds Symphony Setup’s two organization permissions Secrets and Variables (read and write), used only in an adoption run to add the adopted repository to the lists of repositories that read the token slots of the organization’s pool owned by the person who asked, by their login and account id, one they lent with no say among them, and, beside one of them, the pool’s two variables, as the section on what each App asks for says; it reads Symphony Setup’s installation on the organization, the settings variable, which names each slot’s owner, and the records of those secrets and of the two variables, the variables’ values among them, and no secret’s value. It says what the public log and the pull request then say, and that the lending stays whatever becomes of the pull request. It says what the run’s public log shows, now with your account id beside your login: both in the settings of the step that names the repository (your login also in the request job’s step that resolves an installation or, for a repository you named, that checks you administer it) and of every later step for a repository you named, and whether the repository belongs to an organization. It also says that the Tokens page writes the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO readable by no repository’s workflows, where version 31 said the private repositories’ workflows could read it, and closes a list an earlier page left readable by them or by every repository. It says too that a token in the organization’s keeping, one lent with no say, is placed by the organization’s owners alone, as the Token workflow has done since symphony-template#254: its lender may delete it, and no longer takes it off a repository or lends it further with an ordinary lend.
