Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 31 adds the control panel’s Notebooks tab, as the section on the control panel says: it reads the drive organizer’s proposal of notebooks and its catalog from the branch drive-catalog of a private repository, and whether each notebook’s repository exists and whether it is private, internal or public, and writes the proposal there, as you, when you propose, change or take out a notebook. It also names the pull request the Agents tab opens to give an agent its token slots and the files it reads for it, accounts.json and tools/pool.py, and the Tokens page’s read of the branch pool, which earlier versions left out, and says, under SymphonyBoard’s Contents permission, that the control panel writes files with it, as you, as the section on the control panel lists: the pull requests it opens, Track on the Folders tab since version 21, and now the Notebooks tab. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 30 adds the control panel’s “Your token” box and the Token workflow’s manage job, which lists, takes back or deletes the one token in an organization’s pool whose settings name you, by your GitHub login and account id, on SymphonyBoard’s installation token; and the two kinds of issue that start the Token workflow without the page, a lend and a manage, which anyone who may open an issue on a repository carrying the workflow may use, the issue’s author being the person the run acts for and the run closing the issue; among them the lend with no say, whose token goes to the repositories the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO names, or nowhere yet, and whose lender is told the slot’s number and that the token is in the organization’s keeping. The settings variable also keeps each token’s account id beside its login and, for such a token, the word organization, which a save on the page now keeps; a token a collaborator adds is lent to the repository it was added on, and where they have a token in the pool already that one is lent and no second one is made. It says that the pool the App writes can only be the developer’s own organization’s, where the App’s key is, whose owners, the developer among them, hold the tokens lent there with each lender’s login and account id; that the Token workflow mints SymphonyBoard’s token with every permission the installation has; that the settings variable reaches every repository a token was ever lent to and is printed in runs’ logs; and that the token is held on the runner in a file until it is sealed. The developer’s collector receives nothing new.

Version 29 says that Symphony Setup no longer uninstalls itself after an adoption or after a request refused because the repository is adopted already: it stays installed, acting only during an adoption run, until you uninstall it. In a repository that takes the whole template, the run also sets GitHub Actions as the only source of the check named “check” in the ruleset it created; to see GitHub Actions report that check, it reads the check runs on the branch symphony/adopt with a SymphonyBoard token limited to Checks read-only for that one repository, revoked when the settings step ends. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 28 adds the one write SymphonyBoard makes of its own: where a collaborator who is not an owner of the organization presses “Add a Claude account”, the organization’s own Token workflow, on the App’s installation token, writes the minted slot as an organization secret and writes the organization variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, so a collaborator can add a Claude slot GitHub would otherwise let only an owner add; the Claude token is sealed before it is written and the App reads and writes no other secret or variable of its own. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 27 adds SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Variables (read and write), for the control panel’s Tokens page on a personal account’s repository, which holds a Claude slot’s settings and the list of accounts as that repository’s own Actions variables, each as you; until the permission is accepted on the App’s installation such a repository takes one Claude token, its main one. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 26 adds the Folders tab’s read of the drive organizer’s catalog, as the section on the Folders tab says: where the repository holds the branch drive-catalog and no drive is connected, the tab reads catalog.json from that branch, with your GitHub token, and shows the folders and files it names; nothing is asked of Microsoft. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 25 adds the Ask Claude bar’s button “Ask in claude.ai”, as the section on the control panel says: it opens claude.ai in a new tab, on your own account, with your question and what the page shows in that tab’s address; the page itself sends nothing. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 24 adds the control panel’s Explore tab, as the section on the control panel says: a map of the repository’s work from its goals and epics down to the runs on a task’s branch, their jobs and steps and a job’s log, read as you only when you go into a level, kept in the open page’s memory and written nowhere. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 23 adds the Folders tab’s list drawn as a file explorer, its read of each item’s path in the drive and web address, and the opening of a file from it, in its Office program on your computer or on OneDrive’s own page, which hands your browser the file’s address and nothing else. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 22 adds the control panel’s reads of the agents’ list .github/symphony/agents.json and the agent files it names, of the repositories its “Add repository” dialog offers, and of the Share tab’s collaborators and waiting invitations, and the writes its cards and the Share tab make on your press, as you: closing an issue as not planned, closing a pull request, a pull request, from a branch of its own, that changes or deletes a worker’s file or deletes an agent’s file and its line in agents.json, and a collaborator’s or an invitation’s new role, removal or withdrawal. The page keeps nothing new. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 21 adds the control panel’s Folders tab, as the section of that name says: a tab of the control panel’s one page, on its sign-in and the repository its bar chooses, that makes a repository of yours track files and folders of your OneDrive; the box Track asks you to tick before it tracks into a public repository, where what comes down and drive.json’s names can be read by anyone; that whoever can run a workflow on the repository can use its secret to reach your whole drive, and how to withdraw the access at Microsoft; SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Secrets (read and write), for the tab and for the Tokens page on a personal account’s repository; the tab’s reads of the repository’s drive.json, of whether its secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH is set and of whether it has drive-sync.yml, and of your newest repositories when you ask it to find the one you just made; Track’s three writes, as you: the secret sealed in your browser, the file drive.json, on a branch with a pull request where the default branch takes only those, and a run of drive-sync.yml; the drive’s consent at Microsoft, which returns to the control panel’s own address, and the sign-in service, which adds the client secret of the developer’s Microsoft app registration, kept on Cloudflare, answers with the drive’s access token and refresh token and keeps nothing; the tokens in the page’s memory alone, for one sitting and one GitHub account; the page’s reads of your drive’s folders through Microsoft Graph, from your browser; the refresh token passing through the service on Connect and, from the repository’s workflow, on every sync, the one exchange the service answers for any caller; and the 90 days a Microsoft refresh token lasts. It also says that the control panel talks to the sign-in service and Microsoft for the Folders tab. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 20 adds the layout the control panel keeps in your browser: the sizes of the panels you resized and the text size you chose, numbers alone, sent nowhere. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 19 adds the control panel’s Dependencies tab, which draws each open epic’s tasks and the issues blocking them, and the goals above their epics: the page’s reads, as you, of the sub-issues of each open issue labelled epic or goal and of the issues blocking each of an epic’s sub-issues, what GitHub’s own issue pages show, made whenever the page reads the repository’s open issues, whether or not the tab is open, at most sixty for one drawing and none once your token has fewer than a hundred calls left in its hour; and the copy of Mermaid that the developer’s site carries, which the page loads only when there is a chart to draw and which also draws the charts of the board’s STATE.md in the Board tab, only those written as the board writes them. The tab keeps what it reads in the open page alone and writes nothing, to GitHub or to your browser. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 18 adds each token’s id and owner in its settings, the page’s read of your role in the organization, the dialog’s list of the repositories a token is on, and the token:<id> label a worker’s run puts on the issue it worked.

Version 17 adds SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Administration (read and write), used only by the control panel’s Share tab to invite a collaborator you name, as you, and the Share tab’s lookup of an email address in GitHub’s user search. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 16 adds the Tokens page’s tiles: the settings each token’s tile writes to the variable SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS and its label variable, and the X that deletes a slot’s secret, label, settings and place in SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 15 says that the Tokens page’s “Add a Claude account” starts the workflow Token on the repository in place of “Add with one press”, which made a Codespace: the issue it opens, the sign-in link, the code and the sealed token on that issue, the page saving the sealed box as the next slot and as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN while that is not set, and the link to the Claude GitHub App’s install page. The page no longer makes a Codespace or saves a Codespaces secret, and the permissions Codespaces and Codespaces user secrets go unused. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 14 adds Symphony Setup’s organization permission Administration (read and write), used only to allow “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” for an organization whose policy holds it off, so the sixth setting needs no step by hand there; the run reads the organization’s workflow permissions to leave the token’s default permissions as they were. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 13 adds SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Actions (read and write), which the control panel’s buttons that start a workflow run by hand, and its reads of the runs, use as you. What the pages do is unchanged, and nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 12 adds the Tokens page’s “Add with one press”: SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Codespaces and account permission Codespaces user secrets; the Codespace the page makes and deletes on your press; the page’s GitHub token handed to it as your Codespaces secret SYMPHONY_GITHUB_HANDOVER, seen by your own Codespaces on that repository alone and deleted once the slot is saved; the Claude token going from claude to GitHub inside the Codespace, never to the page; and the page’s reads of the organization’s secret names while it waits. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 11 adds the control panel’s Assistant section: an issue of yours, Assistant: <your login> labelled assistant, that the page opens once per repository on your press, each question a comment of yours on it that mentions @claude and ends with a short block of the page’s state, the answer the repository’s Claude workflow writes there, reading only, the page’s reads of that issue’s comments every few seconds while it waits, its reads of whether you may write to the repository and of the assistant’s file on the default branch, and the number of that issue kept in your browser for each repository. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 10 adds SymphonyBoard’s two organization permissions, Secrets and Variables (read and write), and the Tokens page’s “Add or renew a slot”, which seals a Claude token you paste in your browser and saves it, as you, as one of your organization’s Actions secrets, with its label and the list of slots as variables. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 9 says where a sign-in for one tab keeps its refresh token: in the open page’s memory alone, never in the browser’s storage, so that the renewals end once that page is closed, reloaded or replaced by another page, and the sign-in then ends with its eight-hour token; that the tab’s own storage comes back with a tab the browser reopens or restores; that a pasted token is asked about at GitHub before the page keeps it; and that a sign-in’s token that a new sign-in or an accepted pasted token replaces is revoked through the service, as “Forget the token” revokes one. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 8 adds the control panel and the cost page of the developer’s site, as the section of that name says: pages that work in your browser with a GitHub token you give them, talk to GitHub’s API as you, and, with “Sign in with GitHub”, send GitHub’s one-time code to a stateless service of the developer’s on Cloudflare that answers with the token and a refresh token and keeps nothing. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 7 removes the sweep: no workflow on the front door lists SymphonyBoard’s installations every ten minutes and reads each repository they reach to decide whether to offer an adoption, since installing the App alone is no longer a request, the install sending you to the form, where the press is; the run reads an installation only when a form carries its number, as the adoption section now says, and the collector’s daily read of the branch metrics is as it was. With the sweep go two things the run did on its path only: it no longer reads a repository’s direct collaborators to find an administrator, since every request names the person who asked, and it no longer opens an issue in your repository when it could not open its pull request, since the form’s own issue is answered instead. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 6 says that the run, asked for a repository with no commit yet, first makes its first commit, as GitHub’s own “Add a README file” does: a README.md holding the repository’s name, on the default branch, which Contents write allows; that it reads whether such a repository has any branch at all; that closing the pull request leaves that README; and, as it did already, that when the form carries an installation’s number the run asks of each repository both Apps reach what it asks of the one it adopts. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 5 says that the run also reads the two switches under their names before the rename to Symphony, .github/sdlc-adopt and .github/sdlc-metrics; that an adoption never turns on a switch of the repository’s own that says off already, under either name, and brings nothing that shares where it cannot write the switch; that a repository adopted before the rename turns sharing off in .github/sdlc-metrics, the switch its workflow reads; and that Symphony Setup also uninstalls itself after a request refused because the repository is adopted already. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 4 adds the sixth setting Symphony Setup applies: in a repository that takes the whole template, it ticks “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” where your organization and its enterprise allow it. It also names what the run reads to leave your settings as they are: the repository’s rulesets, its topics and its workflow permissions for GitHub Actions. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.

Version 3 adds to METRICS.json what the work cost, as the section on field metrics describes: the tokens Claude used, by kind and by model family, their price at Anthropic’s API list prices and the date of that list, the seconds Claude was at work, the counts and rates per merge they are set against, and the comparison of work done alone with work done in parallel; and it says which records in your repository the workflow reads to make them, and that the switch stops those records too. Nothing else changed.

Version 2 adds to METRICS.json and JUDGE.json the counts of how the work ran in parallel that the section on field metrics describes, and to JUDGE.json how many of its conversations had two or more people, the number of days it covered and any limit it ran under. It also says what the workflow reads to make METRICS.json, and names what the two files held already and version 1 left out: the time each was made, the number of days METRICS.json covers and the short id of the protocol’s commit, and, in JUDGE.json, how many conversations were judged, the totals of the failure types’ three groups, the model, the version of the prompt and the word that names its schema. Nothing else changed.

Symphony is not a GitHub or Anthropic product. “GitHub” is GitHub’s mark; “Claude” and “Claude Code” are Anthropic’s marks, used here to say what Symphony works with.
